items.cleanReaderHtml:
“Mighty Miniatures,” an exhibition celebrating the intricate art of miniatures, is on view at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian in New York from Saturday, November 21 through Friday, August 20, 2027. Curated by Anya Montiel (Tohono O’odham descent), the exhibition features over 300 pieces of art that showcase the skill of Indigenous weavers, sculptors, carvers and other artists that work on a miniscule scale.

The exhibition includes tiny masterpieces created over a span of nearly two centuries by artists from Indigenous communities from North and South America, as well as Hawai'i and the Caribbean. The small works reflect worldviews and cultural expressions, encouraging play and transferring intergenerational knowledge. 

“‘Mighty Miniatures’ brings together some of the smallest works in the museum collection, reaching across the Western Hemisphere and spanning nearly 200 years,” Montiel said. “It is amazing to see how these miniatures have been made with such skill, ingenuity, and detail. This exhibition is a celebration of Indigenous artistry on a small scale and the artists who create them.”

The exhibition is divided into six sections: 

  • Playing with Scale introduces visitors to the concept of miniatures, placing small works alongside their full-sized equivalents.
  • Play Is Important! highlights miniatures as essential teaching tools for children to learn about their world and practice adult skills, and includes cradleboards, mother and child figures, dolls, and clothing. 
  • Watercraft shows Indigenous models of canoes, kayaks, and other vessels designed to navigate rivers, lakes, and oceans across the Americas. 
  • Architecture reflects a diversity of Indigenous housing styles and materials to refute the stereotype that “all Indians live in tipis” with examples from the Northern Cheyenne, Navajo, Zuni, Yupik, Iñupiaq, and Kichwa peoples. 
  • Skill and Artistry explains one of the reasons why Indigenous artists make miniatures. It is a way for artists to showcase their mastery of materials and techniques.  
  • Tourism and the Art Market features some miniatures that have become collectible works of art, like Alaskan ivory carvings and Maine fancy baskets, with people seeking miniatures for their personal collections. 

A family-friendly opening program is scheduled for Saturday, Dec. 12, 11 AM–4 PM. Multi-disciplinary artist Lance Cardinal (Cree), a finalist on the TV show Best In Miniature, will lead visitors in mini drum making sessions. Gallery tours by Montiel will illuminate the stories behind the objects and discuss how the exhibition came together. 

Plan your visit and get tickets at AmericanIndian.si.edu.

items.title: Tate Turns Julio Le Parc Into Instagram Art
items.author: Natalie Weis
items.summary: The show elides the artist’s political motivations, instead cheerfully encouraging visitors to “let these mesmerizing works engage your senses.”

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic

Tate Turns Julio Le Parc Into Instagram Art
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Natalie Weis
Tate Turns Julio Le Parc Into Instagram Art

items.cleanReaderHtml:
LONDON — In Paris, in the years leading up to the massive social upheavals of 1968, Julio Le Parc was making the first of his Game Rooms. These were collections of works that aimed to playfully destabilize the viewer’s experience, such as seats with springs that challenged the act of sitting, areas of uneven tile floors, and patterned discs designed to be manually spun. But for Le Parc, as well as the progressive collective Groupe de Recherche d’Art Visuel (GRAV) that he co-founded, the works were about far more than entertainment. Indeed, he hoped that cultivating the audience’s active participation would not only disrupt what he saw as the hierarchical and passive nature of the museum, but also effect a political awakening outside of it.

A recreation of one of the Game Rooms appears in the exhibition Julio Le Parc: Light. Colour. Action., which was “developed in close dialogue with the artist,” before his death earlier this year at the age of 97. Though the current world, as in 1960s Paris, grapples with mounting social and political tensions, one is unlikely to describe today’s art museum experience as “passive.” Indeed, outgoing Tate Modern Interim Director Catherine Wood notes in the exhibition catalog’s foreword, “At a time of heightened popularity for exhibitions touting immersive and interactive experiences, celebrating Julio Le Parc’s seven-decade career with a monographic exhibition at Tate Modern feels especially meaningful and urgent.”

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Come November and December, northerly climes brace for dropping temperatures and the first snow. Winter may not be everyone’s favorite, and it’s easy to dwell on gray days and leafless trees. Fortunately, when the sun shines, the cold months can also reveal abundant life and beauty, and many woodland denizens thrive during this time of the year. It’s a side of the season that photographer Roeselien Raimond expresses in her series Zen & The Art of Winter Foxes.

Raimond documents serene vulpine creatures in moments of repose amid peaceful, snowy surrounds. “The images are part of a personal project about the unexpected connection between nature, photography and inner peace,” the artist tells Colossal. “The idea originated from an encounter with a vixen during a snowstorm, when I found myself feeling completely at ease despite the freezing conditions.”

Meeting the reclusive animal spurred an ongoing series and exploration of the Zen paradox of desire, in which the search for something can make it more difficult to find. Raimond taps into nature’s powerful lesson that quietude and mindfulness can help us to recharge, just like the foxes’ natural inclination to rest, reflect, and simply soak up some rays. See more on Instagram.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
While it sounds like something from a sci-fi movie, “hyperparasitism” is a legit scientific term for when a parasite infects another parasite (as if one parasite wasn’t trouble enough). Although apparently widespread, the phenomenon is little studied. A recent paper published in Proceedings of the Royal Society B detailed the relationship between the fungi that cause powdery mildew in plants and another fungus ( Ampelomyces spp.) that piggybacks on it.

The powdery mildew fungi (family Erysiphaceae) are infamous in the agricultural industry, since they’re obligate parasites—i.e., they can only survive on living plant tissue—of many crops, including wheat, grapes, and soybeans. In all, they attack 10,000 species of flowering plants. When you add Ampelomyces to the equation in a “parasite-on-parasite system,” however, crops have a better chance at survival.

“By understanding hyperparasite diversity and how many different strains are out there, it might give us insights on if some are better at controlling the fungus than others,” explained senior study author Michael Bradshaw, an entomologist and plant pathologist at North Carolina State University, in a press release .

Powdery mildews can’t be cultured, and so, Bradshaw and coauthors screened 609 samples of dried powdery mildews from herbarium specimens originally collected from 28 countries over the last 150 years. Hyperparasites can’t easily be detected with the naked eye, but DNA sequencing, followed by microscopy, revealed the presence of Ampelomyces parasites on 40 specimens. 671 more Ampelomyces gene sequences were found in the genetic repository GenBank.

This hyperparasite turns out to be much more common than previously thought, with about seven percent of all powdery mildews examined in the study carrying Ampelomyces. It was also more diverse than expected, with five distinct genera encompassing 47 different strains, including some possible new species. “Collectively, these results highlight the evolutionary and ecological complexity of the Ampelomyces -powdery mildew system,” wrote the study authors.

There’s not just a fungus among us—there are fungi on fungi.

Devin Reese is the executive editor of Natural History and a science writer based in Alexandria, Virginia.

items.title: More Than a Billion Years' Worth of Rock Layers Are Missing From Earth's Geologic Record. Scientists Say They May Finally Know Why
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: Computer simulations suggest that movements in Earth's viscous mantle layer lifted certain chunks of the planet's surface, allowing ice sheets to scrape away the rock

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Margherita Bassi
YouTube Logo

videos.caption: Enlace audiovisual citado en la nota

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Rock layers record the Earth’s history, typically piling up from oldest at the bottom to youngest at the top. But a giant, mysterious gap exists in many of the globe’s landmasses. It’s well-documented in North America, northern Europe and northern China, where in some places more than one billion years of our planet’s geologic record is nowhere to be found.

Now, scientists say they may have figured out what caused the so-called Great Unconformity.

Computer simulations hint the missing rock layers, which should be older than roughly 540 million years old, were uplifted by movements of Earth’s viscous mantle layer and eroded away by giant ice sheets before the continents sank back down again. The findings, published November 4 in the journal Nature , help validate some of the possible explanations about the Great Unconformity, possibly solving the 150-year-old mystery.

“Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth’s story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story,” says study co-author Santosh Dhungana , an Earth scientist at the University of Wollongong in Australia, in a statement . “Our research suggests these pages weren’t lost by chance.”

Researchers first described the Great Unconformity in the late 1800s in the layers of the Grand Canyon .

Many scientists suspect that during the planet’s theorized Snowball Earth period, when the entire planet may have been frozen some 635 million to 720 million years ago, moving ice scraped away the missing rock layers. But if ice sheets covered the globe, they should have eroded the Great Unconformity everywhere, which isn’t the case, reports Ars Technica ’s Jacek Krywko.

Some researchers have also hypothesized that mantle movements, which alter the planet’s surface, could be to blame. In the viscous mantle, hotter material rises and cooler material falls, pushing and pulling Earth’s outer layer, called the crust. However, this concept of mantle-driven dynamic topography “hadn’t been quantitatively tested,” study co-author Nicolas Flament , a geoscientist at the University of Wollongong, tells Ars Technica .

So, he and Dhungana used computer models to simulate these mantle movements, called convection, over the past billion years. Their six models “consistently showed that mantle convection caused ancient continental blocks Laurentia (which now makes up much of North America), Baltica (parts of northern Europe) and North China to be lifted up from around a billion years ago to 540 million years ago,” the authors write for the Conversation . Over the past 540 million years, however, these continental chunks have sunk.

The era of continental uplift overlaps with the Snowball Earth period, and giant moving ice sheets erode landscapes more efficiently than rivers. The scientists speculate that the frozen masses would have ground their way down the slopes of raised landscapes, wiping away millions of years’ worth of rock accumulation.

What’s more, the Great Unconformity intrigues scientists interested in life’s history because it wiped the rock record just before the Cambrian explosion around 530 million years ago, when all sorts of animals suddenly evolved.

The geologic processes that took place during the Great Unconformity may have created the foundation for this famous evolutionary event, Shanan Peters , a geoscientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who did not participate in the study, tells Live Science ’s Stephanie Pappas. By exposing older crystalline rocks, for example, the erosion may have triggered a greater release of certain elements, such as potassium, iron, manganese and carbon, into the oceans, allowing marine life to invent shells. That, in turn, may have put more oxygen into Earth’s atmosphere, Peters adds.

“Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see,” Flament says in the statement.

Margherita Bassi is a freelance journalist and trilingual storyteller. Her work has appeared in publications including BBC Travel, Discover magazine, Live Science , Atlas Obscura and Hidden Compass .

items.title: Draconian Trump Executive Order Could Strip Art Orgs of Nonprofit Status
items.author: Anna Lee
items.summary: The order under consideration would strip all nonprofit organizations with alleged “terrorist ties” of their tax-exempt status.

images.caption: Lámina de Hyperallergic
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Anna Lee
Draconian Trump Executive Order Could Strip Art Orgs of Nonprofit Status

items.cleanReaderHtml:
After the Wall Street Journal reported earlier this month that the White House is considering an executive order that would strip nonprofits deemed to have alleged "terrorist ties" of their tax-exempt status, many arts and culture organizations are bracing for what could be a series of politically targeted attacks from the Trump administration.

According to the report, officials are reviewing Section 501(p)(2)(C) of the United States Internal Revenue Code, which authorizes the president to label nonprofits that are allegedly "supporting or engaging in terrorist activity." Organizations tagged with the label would have their tax-exempt status immediately suspended, spelling a potentially devastating blow to their operations.

The White House has not made an official confirmation or announcement of the measure, with a spokesperson telling Hyperallergic that "any policy announcements will come directly from the President," and "discussions about potential decisions or their impacts are otherwise baseless speculation."

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Conjure an image of a basket in your mind. Is it made of straw, or perhaps sweetgrass or willow? Does it have a handle? Was it made by hand, and what could it hold? At Mindy Solomon Gallery, a forthcoming exhibition titled Interwoven: Basketry As Expanded Practice challenges our perception of both object and craft.

Curated by Dee Clements, the exhibition considers the way basketmaking techniques are far from limited to the splinted white ash trug we might carry out to the garden or the simple vessel that holds recipes in the kitchen. This vibrant survey “breaks craft tradition,” a statement says, positioning the practice as an art form. The show asks “what happens when basketry is understood not as a fixed category of craft, but as an open-ended artistic language?”

The artists in Interwoven use a range of materials, from ceramic and steel to cotton and paper. Salvador Dominguez’s vibrant pipe cleaner vessels are complemented by wall works like Eric Gushee’s intricately interlaced wire sculptures and Miguel Arzabe’s woven, deconstructed paintings.

Viewers will find further explorations by artists like Dienke Dekker and José Santiago Pérez, who work with unexpected materials like paper and emergency blankets, respectively. And Colossal readers might also recognize work by Xanthe Somers and Sonia Barrett, among the nearly two dozen participating artists.

Interwoven opens on November 29 and continues through January 9 in Miami. See more on the gallery’s Instagram.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
With substantial scholarships, exceptional facilities, accomplished faculty, and private studios, students pursuing an MFA in Studio Art and Design at the University of Louisville have the resources and creative freedom to develop their artistic practice within a dynamic, supportive community.

The rigorous 60-credit MFA program encourages experimentation, critical inquiry, and interdisciplinary exploration. Students may pursue interdisciplinary practices or concentrate on individual media, including ceramics, drawing, glass, painting, photography, printmaking, sculpture, design, new media, and installation.

Located in Louisville's Portland arts district, the MFA program occupies a dedicated, newly renovated warehouse featuring individual graduate studios, state-of-the-art production facilities, laboratories, a seminar room, and an exhibition gallery. This distinctive environment provides students with the space, resources, and opportunities to develop ambitious creative projects.

The Hite Institute also offers a 31-credit-hour MA in Art History or Curatorial Studies. Combining critical theory, art historical research, contemporary art, and hands-on exhibition experience, the program prepares students for careers in museums, galleries, curatorial practice, arts administration, and art writing, as well as further academic study.

Founded in 1946, the endowed Hite Institute of Art + Design has built a distinctive identity grounded in its avant-garde origins and oriented to creative experimentation and critical inquiry. Its accomplished faculty of practicing artists, designers, and scholars encourages students to expand their creative and intellectual horizons while engaging with contemporary cultural, social, and environmental issues.

Both graduate programs maintain small, selective cohorts, allowing for close faculty mentorship, individualized attention, and meaningful collaboration. Students benefit from the Hite Institute's extensive resources, including six galleries, outstanding glass and additive manufacturing facilities, partnerships with museums and cultural institutions, an active alumni network, and visiting lectures by internationally recognized artists, curators, and arts professionals.

In addition to guaranteed scholarships, graduate students may qualify for teaching assistantships, internships, and additional awards that provide valuable professional experience and support their creative and scholarly development.

Applications for Fall 2027 admission are due January 15, 2027.

To learn more, visit art.louisville.edu

items.author: Charlie Wood
items.summary: An era-defining galaxy survey has released its final results. They don’t quite fit the leading theory of cosmology. The post What Makes Up the Cosmos? A 20-Year Survey Hints That Something Is Missing. first appeared on Quanta Magazine

The 570-megapixel Dark Energy Camera is mounted on the Victor M. Blanco 4-Meter Telescope on Cerro Tololo near La Serena, Chile.

Dark Energy Survey/DOE/FNAL/ DECam/CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA

J oshua Frieman remembers when the world found out that the universe was made of much more than just matter. For a few years, the scientist had been studying the possibility that the cosmos needed something else — a “missing energy” — to make sense. But it was a niche idea. When he and a colleague started to plan a workshop on the topic in 1997, at first only a few dozen people signed up. Then, in early 1998, two teams of researchers announced that exploding stars called supernovas seemed to be racing away from Earth under the influence of an unidentified, omnipresent repellent force. The observations implied the existence of exactly the sort of missing energy that Frieman and his colleagues planned to talk about.

“Suddenly, everyone wanted to come to our workshop,” including reporters with TV cameras, said Frieman, now at the University of Chicago. It was “kind of a circus.”

Within a few years, cosmologists had arrived at a whole new view of reality. The missing energy, given the name “dark energy” for its invisible nature, was pushing galaxies apart. The energy seemed embedded in space itself. It made up roughly two-thirds of creation (with matter — visible and dark — making up the remainder). Frieman embarked on what would become a two-decade mission to learn about dark energy by watching how it influences all that we can see: the Dark Energy Survey (DES).

Now that project has come to a close. In May 2026, DES shared findings based on its full dataset of thousands of supernovas and hundreds of millions of galaxies spanning billions of years of cosmic history. Those findings, in combination with data gathered by a different project, the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI), suggest that our understanding of what the universe is made of — the venerable “standard model” of cosmology — is not complete. “There appear to be cracks in that model,” said Simone Ferraro , a cosmologist at Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. “There’s something that doesn’t fit.”

Joshua Frieman, a physicist at the University of Chicago, co-founded the Dark Energy Survey to examine the accelerating expansion of the universe.

Cosmologists can’t yet say what that something is. What they can say is that after 20 years of stability, their field is returning to a state of confusion. “It’s certainly enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited,” Ferraro said.

Experimental cosmology is a piecemeal endeavor. It’s a bit like trying to reconstruct a person’s life from a dossier of data about them: report cards, utility bills, cholesterol tests, and so on. You come up with a story that weaves all the data together, go find new data, and use it to refine the story. Frieman and other cosmologists started to speculate about a missing form of energy in the mid-1990s because the story they were telling didn’t seem quite right.

In previous decades, they had peered at the sky and inferred roughly how much stuff was out there. They saw a smattering of galaxies lighting up the void — visible matter. Based on how fast the galaxies were spinning, astronomers deduced that a preponderance of invisible matter must surround each bright speck, holding it together — dark matter.

It’s certainly enough to make you either uncomfortable or excited.

The rate at which these galaxies were receding from view implied that the universe had been expanding for some 8 billion to 13 billion years. It looked as if there was just enough matter (dark and visible combined) to tug gravitationally on the universe and continuously slow this expansion without ever bringing it to a full halt.

But new observations started to clash with this accounting. Astronomers spotted stars, for instance, that seemed to be older than the universe. While trying to understand these and other anomalies, cosmologists noticed that it helped to add a new type of energy to their models.

items.title: Europe's Hera Spacecraft Has Begun Its Close-Up Investigation of the Asteroid System NASA Intentionally Hit in 2022
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: The European Space Agency's mission will provide valuable data about the aftermath of the planned collision, which can inform planetary defense measures and reveal insights about asteroids

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Sara Hashemi
image of an asteroid with a smaller, shadowed rock below

items.cleanReaderHtml:
The European Space Agency (ESA) has started its close-up investigation of an asteroid system smashed by NASA in 2022.

ESA’s Hera spacecraft reached the Didymos binary asteroid system on November 4, more than two years after it launched from Cape Canaveral, Florida. The mission will examine the aftermath of NASA’s Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) collision, helping scientists better understand how the technique could one day be used to protect Earth from incoming space rocks.

The asteroid Didymos is roughly 2,560 feet in diameter and has a companion moonlet called Dimorphos, which is about 495 feet in diameter. They form a binary asteroid system , a pair of asteroids that are gravitationally bound, orbiting each other around a shared center of mass.

In September 2022, the golf-cart-size DART spacecraft intentionally struck the smaller celestial body in the world’s first demonstration of asteroid deflection technology. The mission not only successfully collided with Dimorphos, shortening its orbit around its big sibling by 33 minutes; it also altered the asteroid pair’s route around the sun . Now, Hera is returning to the crash scene to follow up on that work.

“Hera wants to be the detective, like Inspector Colombo, going back to the crash scene,” Patrick Michel , a planetary scientist at the French National Center for Scientific Research and Hera’s principal investigator, tells Meghan Bartels for Space.com .

The spacecraft, which is about the size of a small car , performed its first arrival maneuver on October 15, and ESA released Hera’s first close-up photo of the asteroid duo on November 5. The picture, snapped about 37 miles from the rocky pair, prominently features Didymos, with the smaller Dimorphos mostly hidden in the larger asteroid’s shadow.

While looking at this image, “the first thing we said was wow!” Michel says in a statement . “This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART’s camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.”

On November 12, ESA released another image of the asteroid system , this time taken from about 35 miles away. It shows one side of Didymos and a sliver of Dimorphos peeking out from behind the larger rock, on the upper left. This photo reveals various features on the bigger asteroid’s surface, including large boulders, smooth areas and a sharp ridge at the equator.

Scientists want to understand which of these and other characteristics were present long ago and which might be consequences of the DART impact.

“Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately one kilometer of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out,” says Michael Küppers , a planetary scientist and Hera mission scientist at ESA, in the earlier statement. “We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.”

Hera should now be within about 20 miles of the asteroid duo, per Space.com , and then move even closer in December. Then, early next year, the spacecraft will deploy two shoebox-size CubeSats . These nanosatellites, equipped with radar and spectral instruments, will fly in and examine the surfaces and inner structures of the asteroids. One of the devices, called Juventas, will attempt to land on Dimorphos to capture more information about the asteroid’s surface material and gravity field.

The DART and Hera missions were intentionally designed to go together , with the first performing the deflection and the second collecting precise measurements of the outcome.

These studies will not just help experts develop techniques for planetary defense in case an object one day poses a danger to Earth; they’ll also advance our understanding of asteroids in general.

“Planetary defense and science are sort of two sides of the same coin,” says Jessica Sunshine , a planetary scientist at the University of Maryland who was on the DART team but is not involved in the Hera mission, to Bartels for Science News . On the science side, she adds, “we’re trying to figure out not so much how did we break the thing, but how was it put together in the first place.”

items.title: The Intricate Textile Designs of William Morris Bring Into Conflict the Concepts of Art and Accessibility
items.author: Smithsonian Arts & Culture
items.summary: The 19th-century craftsman extolled the universal right to beauty. The problem was that his handmade items were necessarily expensive

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Arts & Culture
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Imagen en alta resolución de la fuente
Amy Crawford
Flora, designed by William Morris and Edward Coley Burne-Jones, made by William Knight, William Sleath and John Martin for Morris & Company,

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Born into a wealthy English family, William Morris (1834-1896) grew up in the countryside, honing a love for nature that found expression in fabric and wallpaper he designed for his successful firm, Morris & Company. An activist as well as an artist and businessman, he loathed the inequity of Victorian society and the soullessness of the industrial age, coming to embrace revolutionary socialism.

But while he believed in a universal right to beauty, his own careful craftsmanship held a certain contradiction, says Amy George, curator of a retrospective of Morris’ original designs opening this month at the Whitworth Art Gallery in Manchester, England. “Anything handmade is expensive,” she notes. “And it should be expensive, because of the labor that goes into it.”

Perhaps ironically, in recent years capitalism has made Morris’ work more accessible, as it has appeared on products from mass-market brands like H&M and Williams Sonoma. In a way, it seems, his goal of art for all may finally have been realized.

This article is a selection from the December 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine

Amy Crawford is a Michigan-based freelance journalist writing about cities, science, the environment, art and education. A longtime Smithsonian contributor, her work also appears in CityLab and the Boston Globe .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Svalbard’s reindeer are leaning on their hardscrabble history to adapt to a global disruption

On my first afternoon in Arctic Svalbard in June 2024, two filmmakers in my guesthouse tell me that reindeer are just outside. I have flown halfway around the world to witness these reindeer, and here they are, under our window. I grab my binoculars and boots, walking into a sudden spring snowstorm to see a small herd of reindeer munching on the tundra.

These are not the majestic flying reindeer of Christmas cards. They are stocky, goat-sized, roly-poly survivors—evolutionary success stories that sparked the central questions of my journey: Why would reindeer come to this inhospitable archipelago where glaciers still cover more than 60 percent of the land? How did they transform their bodies and behaviors to thrive in one of Earth’s harshest environments? And as climate change warms Svalbard faster than almost anywhere on Earth, what hope do they have?

We often tell a simple story about Arctic wildlife: as the climate warms, cold-adapted animals disappear. Svalbard’s reindeer suggest a more hopeful and more complicated one. They are not passive victims of climate change. They explore new foods, shift their movements, pass knowledge to their young, and change their bodies over generations. They appear to have agency. And if that’s true, it changes what we might do to help them.

I spent a month on the archipelago, part of it aboard the three-masted Antigua with the Arctic Circle Residency, a floating gathering of artists, scientists, filmmakers, and journalists reflecting on climate and environmental futures. Before and after the residency, I stayed at Mary-Ann’s Polarrig, a funky guesthouse decorated with walrus penises and old mining photographs, where Polish glaciologists waited for the waves to calm and the daughter of a Chukchi reindeer herder staffed the front desk.

At first glance, Svalbard seems like a poor bet for any land mammal. The soil is thin and starved of nutrients, and the sparse browse can’t feed many mouths. In the brief summer that punctuates the winter darkness, reindeer roam through High Arctic valleys in small groups, grazing on grasses, forbs, and tiny willow shrubs in the few ice-free lowlands. Winter is particularly challenging. Polar bears and whales can dive beneath the pack ice to find food, but when the darkness comes, reindeer must crater through the snow for mosses and lichens.

Svalbard’s food web is pared down to the basics. Little auks fertilize the tundra with their droppings, reindeer eat the resulting vegetation, and when they die, Arctic foxes feast on the carcasses. With few predators, weather becomes the main variable shaping populations, which turns the archipelago into a natural laboratory for understanding climate impacts elsewhere.

Isolated for millennia, Svalbard reindeer face a climate paradox. Warming temperatures extend summer growing seasons, allowing reindeer to pack on more calories before winter. But although they double their fat during summer and subsist on those reserves for part of winter, eventually they must forage. If winter rain falls and freezes, ice can form a shell three feet thick over lichen. Reindeer hooves, evolved for cratering through snow, cannot pierce this frozen armor. Many starve. In poor years with winter rain, adult females who survive until spring weigh only around 103 pounds—less than some dogs. In winters without rain, they can weigh 126 pounds.

Reindeer have always survived the occasional rainy winter, often by miscarrying a pregnancy to save the mother. But two rainy winters in a row make survival precarious, and the effects ripple outward to voles, ptarmigan, and foxes.

On my third day, I climbed Sarkofagan, one of the mountains ringing Longyearbyen, Svalbard’s main settlement. Polar bears roam, so you must always hike with an armed guide. Mine was Maria, an Italian geologist finishing a master’s thesis on permafrost.

At the summit cairn, Maria pointed across the fjord to ancient shorelines etched nearly 260 feet above today’s coast, relics of an Arctic shaped by the chaotic transition between the most recent expansion of the ice and our current epoch, the Holocene. Around ten thousand years ago, vast ice sheets retreated, meltwater flooded the oceans, and ice-dammed lakes failed catastrophically, sending walls of water across the landscape. The Polish scientists waiting out the waves at my guesthouse have documented 134 glacial lake drainage events.

I asked Maria why reindeer might come to such a volatile place, and she shrugged. Rocks, she told me, change for predictable reasons, which is why she studies them. Mammals rarely follow laws, scientific or political.

What we do know comes from genetics and archaeology. Svalbard’s reindeer originated in what’s now Russia, and perhaps seven thousand years ago, some individuals crossed the 35 miles of the Kara Strait to Novaya Zemlya, the anvil-shaped archipelago curving into the Arctic Ocean. Some later trekked about 220 miles over pack ice to Franz Josef Land. When glaciers advanced thirteen hundred years ago, most of the reindeer died out, but a few migrated again, trekking roughly 160 miles across sea ice to Svalbard, where the Gulf Stream makes the climate slightly milder.

But could reindeer really cross that distance on pack ice? It seemed impossible, until in 1912, a hunter shot a Svalbard reindeer with an ivory gull’s foot tied to its left antler. This individual had walked over from Novaya Zemlya, where Indigenous Nenets herders marked their reindeer that particular way. The decorated reindeer proved reindeer could make the long crossing on pack ice. But it doesn’t explain why they made that journey.

items.title: These London Apartments Look Straight Out of the Stone Age. Could They Be the Future of Sustainable Architecture?
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: A new residential complex with a load-bearing exoskeleton made from 1,000 tons of raw stone is offering an alternative to carbon-intensive steel and concrete structures. Its designers think that the monumental stone buildings of the past are coming back into fashion

images.caption: Imagen principal de Smithsonian Smart News

Celtic designs
Rooftop gardens

items.cleanReaderHtml:
From low-carbon concrete to mass timber to green steel , architects across the globe are employing cutting-edge technology to revolutionize eco-friendly building design. But the team behind a new north London apartment complex argues the industry’s path forward may lie in the ways of the past.

With a hulking, pink exoskeleton decorated with Celtic patterns, Petra Heights , a trio of apartment towers ranging from six to 10 stories, looks straight out of the Stone Age . That’s fitting, as the development’s load-bearing structures and decorative cladding are one and the same: stacks of raw, unchiseled stone.

“All of the weight of the building is coming down the stone, and all the wind load is carried by the stone,” the project’s engineer, Steve Webb , co-founder of engineering firm Webb Yates , tells Dezeen ’s Jennifer Hahn. Altogether, the complex houses a ground-floor storefront, two rooftop gardens and 22 apartments.

Petra Heights is part of an ongoing collaboration between architecture firm Groupwork , headed by Amin Taha , and Webb Yates to popularize stone as a viable alternative to steel and cement, which together represent 16 percent of global greenhouse gas emissions.

The stone frame—made of pink basalt from Sicily and larvikite from Norway—produces fewer carbon emissions than traditional steel-and-concrete models. With a stone external frame and a concrete internal frame, the Petra Heights project produced around 30 percent less carbon emissions than a fully steel or concrete alternative, the Guardian ’s Oliver Wainwright reports. Those savings could rise to 95 percent with domestically-mined stone, per Dezeen .

The two men began looking into stone 15 years ago after running into roadblocks while collaborating on a steel frame. A conservation officer pointed them towards stone. Skeptical, they asked a stonemason about the feasibility of building with the material, the Architect's Newspaper ’s Richard Martin reports.

“Are you completely stupid?” Webb recalls the mason saying, according to the Architect’s Newspaper . “Just look around London—it’s been all stone for the last one thousand years. It’s still standing. Of course you can build in stone.”

Since then, they have continually pushed the edge of what stone and wood can do. In 2021, the pair’s six-story 15 Clerkenwell Close , featuring a load-bearing stone structure, was shortlisted for the Stirling Prize , the United Kingdom’s most prestigious architecture award. Petra Heights is their biggest concept yet.

To demonstrate the strength and flexibility of stone, Webb Yates, in collaboration with the Stonemasonry Company , designed Stone Space Frame , a nearly 15-foot-tall electricity pylon prototype which requires steel only for tension.

The project used 1,000 tons of rock to form nearly 600 stone columns and lintels. It also features the world’s first fully stone elevator shaft. With no steel reinforcement or secondary structure, Petra Heights is the largest load-bearing stone structure since the great stone cathedrals , the project’s website boasts . And Webb and Ahan aren’t stopping there.

“If we build another one, it can be taller, higher, stronger,” Webb tells Dezeen . In 2020, the duo released a concept for a 30-story office block with a stone exoskeleton.

Currently, Groupwork is working on another stone-bearing mixed-use development in east London. Combined with dowel-laminated timber walls and floors, photovoltaic panels and a canal water source heat pump, the structure will generate 135 percent of its energy needs, making it “ carbon negative ” by selling energy back to the grid.

Webb’s next venture is a 650-foot stone skyscraper sans the usual concrete core and columns. It will feature heavy, dark granite at the base and lighter, thinner limestone towards the top, optimizing the different load-bearing features of the two stones.

“The impact of removing the concrete core from high rises has a big carbon benefit,” Webb tells Dezeen . But he says the next big push of load-bearing stone structures may be even better focused on smaller buildings, particularly as the United Kingdom pushes to deliver on its promise to build 1.5 million new homes before 2029 . “Get rid of all the brickwork, get rid of all the concrete cores from concrete medium rise housing, [that] will put a big dent in the carbon footprint of the million homes," he adds.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
“We are looking at something that no one else has seen before”

It looks like some kind of distant alien world, but it’s actually something much smaller and closer to home.

For the first time, scientists have been able to capture detailed images of the poles at the end of rod-shaped bacteria—with the breakthrough coming not from a new type of camera or scanner but from being able to keep the small microbes still and alive for long enough.

Read more: “ ‘Zombie Bacteria’ Might One Day Lurk in the Sewers ”

The process is detailed in a new study published in Nature Communications , and it involved sticking E. coli bacteria to glass via a substance called glutaraldehyde, which binds to proteins on the surface of bacteria. Crucially, the chemical keeps the bacteria alive, preserving their structure.

From there, they could be scanned using atomic force microscopy, a technique where a probe just a few nanometers wide taps along the cell to image it. The researchers compare it to a human finger reading braille.

Even with this new technique, the snapshot required patience. It took 20 minutes for the stickiness to take effect on the organisms, and 50 minutes to find some of the trapped bacteria standing upright.

It’s been a long journey to get here, too. Getting bacteria to stand up straight for a photo has proved elusive across many experiment types. It’s worthy quest, though, as a look at the poles provides important information about the parts of these tiny cells that are used for growth and defense.

“Imaging the poles of bacteria is like opening a view of the back of the moon,” study author Bart Hoogenboom explained in a statement . “We’re looking at something that no one else has seen before. The poles are where cells divide, and so, (they) contain critical information about this process. They may also be a particular target for antibiotics, with some bacteria-killing treatments preferring to attack this part of the cell.”

With some of the most dangerous pathogens on the planet becoming increasingly resistant to our best drugs, these photos could help develop more effective treatments that attack specific vulnerabilities in the “armor” of the bacteria. And now that they’ve found an imaging approach that works, the researchers say it could be adapted to work over longer timescales as well—capturing processes like successive cell divisions and biofilm formations.

All of which is to say, there are a lot of other microbe poles to image—and many more brand new sights to analyze.

David Nield has written about science and technology for more than 20 years. His work has appeared in a wide range of publications, including Wired, Popular Science, The Guardian , and Gizmodo .

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In Fort Worth, Texas, a massive, dilapidated building serves as an ever-present symbol of racial violence and segregation to those who know its history. Constructed in the 1920s, the structure, initially known as Klavern No 101 , was briefly the auditorium and headquarters of Fort Worth’s Ku Klux Klan chapter. It stood between downtown and the North Side, where migrants and communities of colour had settled, so many residents had to pass it on their way to work. In this short documentary, the director Chris Neighbors, a member of the Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma, brings together scholars, community members and those directly involved in redesigning the space to reflect on its past and the thinking behind its transformation into an arts and community centre. Filmed inside the building itself, their conversations consider a question that extends far beyond Fort Worth: how do we preserve difficult histories without preserving the values they once stood for?

items.author: Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene
items.summary: Civilisation wasn’t made possible by grain, but by transportation – and the conquest it enabled, from the steppe to the sea - by Lhamsuren Munkh-Erdene Read on Aeon

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A horse rider at the market place in Urga (now Ulaanbaatar), Mongolia, photographed by Stéphane Passet in July 1913. Courtesy the Musée Albert-Kahn, France

is professor of history and anthropology at the National University of Mongolia. He is also a visiting scholar with the Mongolia and Inner Asia Studies Unit (MIASU) at the University of Cambridge, UK. He is the author of The Taiji Government and the Rise of the Warrior State: The Formation of the Qing Imperial Constitution (2022) and The Nomadic Leviathan: A Critique of the Sinocentric Paradigm (2023).

Transportation is the backbone of civilisation, which is why controlling the Strait of Hormuz grants global leverage. Because oil fuels more than 90 per cent of global transit, the source of this power lies not in the waterway, but in the control of global mobility. Halting all oil supplies paralyses virtually all transport, communication and supply lines: cities collapse, states disintegrate, societies break down and populations die off, throwing humanity back to the pre-industrial age. Without transport animals, humanity would still be back in the Stone Age.

No city or state can exist without transportation, for there can be no concentration of population and resources. No transportation means no extrahuman transportation, leaving walking and carrying as the only means of transit. This baseline determined the size and structure of human communities. Production was limited to what could be carried home, circumscribing the areas where humans could settle and colonise. Production capacity and resource availability kept communities small, forcing them to split and disperse. Because size dictates structure, small meant undifferentiated and egalitarian. Ultimately, the inherent limit of the physical capability of travel and portage formed a natural immunity to inequality: it kept communities small, egalitarian and autonomous, leaving their lands beyond conquest.

As long as this constraint existed, communities resembled those of the Amazon Basin or the New Guinea Highlands. The domestication of animals and the invention of boats liberated humanity, making long-distance mobilisation possible. With this newfound capacity, communities no longer needed to fit their immediate environments; instead, they could build cities and integrate expansive areas – all roads lead to Rome. Transportation – not grain – is what brought the state and civilisation into existence, and what continues to maintain them. Let’s examine this power by looking from the present back to the origin of the state.

Contemporary live marine traffic map available at marinetraffic.com

W hoever rules the waves rules the world! Without its navy and air force, the United States cannot command global reach or project power worldwide. The same was true of European colonial empires; ultimately, warships and gunboats forged them. In earlier periods, Vikings built their empire on longships, Aztecs on canoes, Egyptians on riverboats, and Romans, Greeks and Phoenicians on galleys.

Conquering the world on horseback is easy, as the saying goes. On land, equids – donkeys and horses – forged states and civilisations, while the llama did the same for the Inkas. Ur’s kunga chariots project the military might of Mesopotamian cities, and the Abydos donkeys demonstrate their vital role in early Egyptian kingship. By the end of the 3rd millennium BCE, Central Eurasian nomads were entombing entire horse chariots – the high-tech, high-value war machines of their time – to honour their kings in Sintashta. Horse chariots later symbolised the power of the Shang and the Zhou; the latter deployed 4,000 chariots to overwhelm the former in 1046 BCE.

Building a state does not require grain, but does demand extrahuman transportation

‘The rider appears on the stage of history like a new breed of man’ – a centaur, as the German sociologist Alexander Rüstow put it in the 1950s. Eurasian nomads had long bred their mounts into the modern domestic horse, paving the way for an age of empires that would fundamentally reshape the world. Horses dominated human history for nearly four millennia. Even for maritime powers, horses remained key to conquest; from Carthage to the British, all relied on horses for inland expansion. Francisco Pizarro’s conquest of the Inkas is a prime illustration of the power of horses against an essentially pedestrian empire built on llama transportation. Horses also enabled the Comanche in North America to forge their empire and compete with European powers for nearly a century.

Comanche warriors, photographed in 1892. Courtesy Wikipedia

The Comanche Empire? Did they actually have grain to build a state? No, they had no grain – nor any agriculture, for that matter. Horse husbandry and bison hunting sustained their livelihood. In fact, all the Eurasian steppe powers – including the Mongols – relied on pastoralism. What they enjoyed most was an abundance of extrahuman transportation; what they lacked most was agricultural produce. Ultimately, building a state does not require grain, but it does demand extrahuman transportation.

Look at the political geography of the Roman and Mongol empires: the Romans could reach where ships could reach, and the Mongols could reach where horses could reach. The same is true of European colonial empires; it all comes down to the power of extrahuman transportation. Donkeys, horses and all other herd animals are the creations of pastoralists. Extrahuman transportation made the state and civilisation possible; this places pastoralism at the origin of the state and civilisation, and the Eurasian steppe at the centre of human history.

The expansion of the Mongol Empire in the 13th century. Courtesy Wikipedia

items.cleanReaderHtml:
It’s a beautiful day to support indie publications! Last week, a survey conducted by Critical Minded and the Rabkin Foundation quantified the precarity of independent US-based art magazines amid a climate of censorship, corporate takeovers, and economic instability. It’s no wonder, when media companies decide to partner with Amazon on art initiatives (cough, cough, Penske). Senior Editor Valentina Di Liscia breaks down the survey results and what they can teach us about the future of independent, critical arts journalism.

Speaking of which, Staff Writer Anna Lee reports on a coalition of Tribal Nations opposing a bill that would threaten Native sites if Congress passes it. Longtime Angeleno Matt Stromberg considers an engrossing if occasionally overwrought book by James Cahill that explores the influential friendship between David Hockney and Betty Freeman, the arts patron at the center of one of his most recognizable paintings. And if that isn’t enough, Aaron Short shares a wry dispatch from the preview of the Art Dealers Association of America’s art fair in New York City — the tickets may have been $250 a pop, but at least there were unlimited dumplings and champagne to sweeten the deal?

—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books

45% of US Independent Arts Publications Face Existential Crisis, Report Finds

Nearly half of independent publications covering arts and culture in the United States said their business models will not be sustainable without “profound changes” to the current funding landscape, according to a report from Critical Minded and the Dorothea and Leo Rabkin Foundation released this week. | Valentina Di Liscia

items.cleanReaderHtml:
When the first Star Wars movie came out, in 1977, cinema was the better part of a century old, yet it had never produced a popular-culture phenomenon on such a scale. Covering the resulting explosion of public enthusiasm, the contemporary media initially struggled to find ways to describe the picture itself. “A cowboy movie set in space, that’s Star Wars,” pronounces the announcer in a TV news clip included in the new Nerdwriter video above. “It’s old-fashioned escapist entertainment, pure and simple.” That may have been all the Italian film industry needed to hear. The “spaghetti westerns” of the previous dozen years had proven that it could profitably master an American genre; surely it could do the same with a similar one.

Among the results, alas, one looks in vain for A Fistful of Dollars, or even a Navajo Joe. Nerdwriter creator Evan Puschak goes over various instances of shameless imitation that characterize the Italian Star Wars clones, but you don’t have to take his word for it; you can, in fact, find some of these movies on YouTube.

Luigi Cozzi’s StarCrash, for example, stars David Hasselhoff, The Spy Who Loved Me Bond girl Caroline Munro, and a Christopher Plummer putting in one of his most grandiosely villainous performances ever; Aldo Lado’s The Humanoid, an even more shameless knock-off, credits its director as “George B. Lewis.” Nor was Italy the only country cashing in on the Star Wars craze: Puschak also shows clips from the Japanese film Message From Space by no less an auteur than Battle Royale director Kinji Fukasaku.

Though many of these second-rate (at best) space operas made money, and some have even retained a certain charm nearly 50 years later, they all come up against the fundamental stinginess of the Cinecittà production model. “The truth is that you can’t imitate Star Wars with a low budget,” says Puschak. Despite all that’s been said about the myriad ways in which it taps into the power of universal myth, “the spectacle, the immersion induced by its groundbreaking special effects, was just as vital to the experience as the story and the characters.” Hard as it may be for today’s young viewers to believe, there was a time when moviegoers weren’t all that discriminating about the realism, or even the plausibility, of the visuals onscreen. After Star Wars, for better or for worse, they’d never overlook visible wires, unsteady lip-sync, or flat matte paintings so easily again.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Leo Tolstoy is remembered as both a towering pinnacle of Russian literature and a fascinating example of Christian anarchism, a mystical version of which the aristocratic author pioneered in the last quarter century of his life. After a dramatic conversion, Tolstoy rejected his social position, the favored vices of his youth, and the dietary habits of his culture, becoming a vocal proponent of vegetarianism in his ascetic quest for the good life. Thousands of his contemporaries found Tolstoy’s example deeply compelling, and several communes formed around his principles, to his dismay. “To speak of ‘Tolstoyism,’” he wrote, “to seek guidance, to inquire about my solution of questions, is a great and gross error.”

“Still,” writes Kelsey Osgood at The New Yorker, “people insisted on seeking guidance from him,” including a young Mahatma Gandhi, who struck up a lively correspondence with the writer and in 1910 founded a community called “Tolstoy Farm” near Johannesburg.

Though uneasy in the role of movement leader, the author of Anna Karenina invited such treatment by publishing dozens of philosophical and theological works, many of them in opposition to a contrary strain of religious and moral ideas developing in the late nineteenth century. Often called “muscular Christianity,” this trend responded to what many Victorians thought of as a crisis of masculinity by emphasizing sports and warrior ideals and railing against the “feminization” of the culture.

Tolstoy might be said to represent a “vegetable Christianity”—seeking harmony with nature and turning away from all forms of violence, including the eating of meat. In “The First Step,” an 1891 essay on diet and ethical commitment, he characterized the prevailing religious attitude toward food:

I remember how, with pride at his originality, an Evangelical preacher, who was attacking monastic asceticism, once said to me “Ours is not a Christianity of fasting and privations, but of beefsteaks.” Christianity, or virtue in general—and beefsteaks!

While he confessed himself “not horrified by this association,” it is only because “there is no bad odor, no sound, no monstrosity, to which man cannot become so accustomed that he ceases to remark what would strike a man unaccustomed to it.” The killing and eating of animals, Tolstoy came to believe, is a horror to which—like war and serfdom—his culture had grown far too accustomed. Like many an animal rights activist today, Tolstoy conveyed his horror of meat-eating by describing a slaughterhouse in detail, concluding:

[I]f he be really and seriously seeking to live a good life, the first thing from which he will abstain will always be the use of animal food, because, to say nothing of the excitation of the passions caused by such food, its use is simply immoral, as it involves the performance of an act which is contrary to the moral feeling—killing.

[W]e cannot pretend that we do not know this. We are not ostriches, and cannot believe that if we refuse to look at what we do not wish to see, it will not exist.… [Y]oung, kind, undepraved people—especially women and girls—without knowing how it logically follows, feel that virtue is incompatible with beefsteaks, and, as soon as they wish to be good, give up eating flesh.

The idea of vegetarianism of course preceded Tolstoy by hundreds of years of Hindu and Buddhist practice. And its growing popularity in Europe and America preceded him as well. “Tolstoy became an outspoken vegetarian at the age of 50,” writes Sam Pavlenko, “after meeting the positivist and vegetarian William Frey, who, according to Tolstoy’s son Sergei Lvovich, visited the great writer in the autumn of 1885.” Tolstoy’s dietary stance fit in with what Charlotte Alston describes as an “increasingly organized” international vegetarian movement taking shape in the late nineteenth century.

Like Tolstoy in “The First Step,” proponents of vegetarianism argued not only against cruelty to animals, but also against “the brutalization of those who worked in the meat industry, as butchers, slaughtermen, and even shepherds and drovers.” But vegetarianism was only one part of Tolstoy’s religious philosophy, which also included chastity, temperance, the rejection of private property, and “a complete refusal to participate in violence or coercion of any kind.” This marked his dietary practice as distinct from many contemporaries. Tolstoy and his followers “made the link between vegetarianism and a wider humanitarianism explicit.”

“How was it possible,” Alston summarizes, “to regard the killing of animals for food as evil, but not to condemn the killing of men through war and capital punishment? Not all members of the vegetarian movement agreed.” Some saw “no connection between the questions of war and diet.” Tolstoy’s philosophical argument against all forms of violence was not original to him, but it resonated all over the world with those who saw him as a shining example, including his two daughters and eventually his wife Sophia, who all adopted the practice of vegetarianism. A book of their recipes was published in 1874, and adapted by Pavlenko for his Leo Tolstoy: A Vegetarian’s Tale. (See one example here—a family recipe for macaroni and cheese.)

In her study Tolstoy and His Disciples, Alston details the Russian great’s wide influence through not only his diet but the totality of his spiritual practices and unique political and religious views. Interestingly, unlike many animal rights activists of his day and ours, Tolstoy refused to endorse legislation to punish animal cruelty, believing that punishment would only result in the perpetuation of violence. “Non-violence, non-resistance and brotherhood were the principles that lay at the basis of Tolstoyan vegetarianism,” she observes, “and while these principles meant that Tolstoyans cooperated closely with vegetarians, they also kept them in many ways apart.”

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Since 2022, astronomers have been puzzling over a new kind of cosmic object called long-period radio transients .

These are objects that emit bright flashes of radio waves into space every few minutes to every few hours.

Some have been traced back to binary systems of a small, dim cool star called a red dwarf in orbit with a star remnant called a white dwarf.

In new research published today in Nature Astronomy, we report the first discovery of a different source for one of these enigmatic intermittent broadcasters: it still involves a white dwarf, but also a star much like our own Sun.

After the discovery of the first long-period radio transient in 2022, once we had ruled out aliens , we went looking for natural explanations.

One idea was that they were extremely slow-spinning neutron star pulsars, the collapsed cores of enormous stars which also send out repeating radio flashes. But in theory a neutron star spinning that slowly shouldn’t produce radio waves, so the answer had to be something else.

When we started traced these radio signals back to their sources, we made a breakthrough. One of our repeating signals came from a red dwarf star, probably orbiting a white dwarf (the remnant of a star like our Sun).

Across the handful of long-period transients whose source stars we can identify, a pattern has emerged: a binary system of a white dwarf and a small, cool red dwarf.

In late 2024, we were looking for new long-period transients using the Murchison Widefield Array radio telescope in Western Australia.

Using a search method developed by PhD student Csanád Horváth , we spotted something: short flashes of radio waves, arriving like clockwork every 7.9 minutes.

Then the flashes stopped. For weeks we saw nothing, and we nearly gave up. But when we plotted every detection and non-detection together, a pattern emerged.

The pulses only appear during a window of about six hours, followed by 26 hours without pulses. The most natural explanation is that the system is a binary: two stars orbiting each other once every 32 hours, with the radio pulses only visible when they are lined up in the right way .

The MeerKAT telescope in South Africa pinpointed the source to a tiny patch of sky containing a single faint star. We turned to the Keck telescope in Hawai’i to record the star’s spectrum – the “fingerprint” of its light, which can tell us a lot about the star itself.

The result was a surprise: this was not a tiny red dwarf, but a G-type star almost the same mass and temperature as our own Sun.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
As far as human history goes, wealth inequality may be a rather recent development. After all, the hunter-gatherer societies we existed in for most of prehistory were generally considered to be more egalitarian than the agricultural-based societies that followed. Now, a new study published in the Journal of Neolithic Archaeology is exploring the roots of this phenomenon focusing on the Corded Ware culture of ancient Bohemia.

The Corded Ware culture—named after the cordlike impressions on the pottery they left behind—existed between roughly 2900 BCE and 2300 BCE throughout much of Europe. In what’s now western Czechia (and elsewhere), the Corded Ware peoples mingled with migrants from the Pontic steppes. The study investigates what happened to wealth inequality in the region by examining how the contents of nearly 300 gravesites changed over time—including the genetics of the deceased.

So how can you tell how rich someone was from their graves?

According to the team, the objects left behind tell the tale. One of the authors developed a tool called QuantWealth, which (as you can probably guess) is a framework for quantifying wealth. The framework assesses the affluence of the deceased by scoring interred objects based on a series of factors—how long they took to manufacture, how scarce they were, how far away they’re from, the weight of any meat offerings, etc.

“Archaeologists have long debated whether steppe populations migrating across Europe from Ukraine brought with them a highly unequal social system and patriarchy,” Mikkel Nørtoft of the University of Copenhagen said in a statement. “Our results suggest a much more dynamic picture, where social differences developed gradually.”

After crunching the numbers, they identified three basic periods. The earliest was a cooperative phase beginning with a volcanic event that cooled global temperatures. During this period, wealth display was relatively muted, and the early settlers appeared to be more focused on forming social cohesion. “In Bohemia, they did this through shared burial rituals, and building earthen mounds, but with few grave goods,” Nørtoft explained.

Between 2,700-2,500 BCE, however, things started to heat up (both literally and figuratively). According to the team, this period was marked by funerary competition. Prestige items (those that were exclusive to certain graves) and meat offerings became more common. They also found that gender inequality grew, as adult male graves became more ostentatiously decorated. A new Y-chromosome haplogroup also appeared during the period, and the researchers suggest the competition may be a sign of patrilineal power struggles.

During the final phase, the new Y-chromosome haplotype dominated and the green shoots of wealth inequality emerged. The team says elaborate burials of a handful of children decorated with copper rings and other ornaments may be indicative of a growing divide between the rich and poor. “The few rich child graves and this prevailing lineage could indicate more inherited wealth and emerging traits of persistent inequality,” Nørtoft said.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
On Madagascar, a furry creature with a puppy-like nose is a key player in pollination. The bat, called the Madagascan flying fox ( Pteropus rufus ), gulps down fruits, flowers, and nectar, resulting in dustings of pollen all over its face. With a wingspan of up to 5 feet, these bats travel as far as 30 miles during their foraging journeys, unwittingly spreading pollen far and wide.

But a new study published in the Journal of Mammalogy shows that Madagascan flying foxes are physically shrinking over time. Biologists who had conducted fieldwork in Madagascar noticed that the flying foxes they observed appeared to be smaller than the ones housed in the mammal collections at the Field Museum in Chicago.

Read more: “ Mother Bats’ Hearts Quicken When They Hear Baby’s Cries ”

“I was thinking about a million different angles to explain why the bats were getting smaller. I wondered if it was related to changes in temperature or habitat,” said lead author Emily Cornelius Rohs, a postdoc at the Field Museum.

Her coauthor Steven M. Goodman, however, had a different hypothesis: commercial hunting. These flying foxes are hunted for meat and are classified by the Malagasy government as a game species. Their population was tallied at about 300,000 in the early 2000s, but continued commercial exploitation has reduced it by about two-thirds.

To see whether the perceived change in body size correlated with the onset of large-scale hunting, Ruhs and Goodman reviewed the Madagascar flying fox collections at nine museums in the U.S. and Europe. They measured the skulls and teeth (the body parts most often preserved) of 121 specimens collected over roughly the last 150 years. Next, they compared pre-hunting and post-hunting sizes.

The results showed a drop in size beginning in about 1980. “If you’re the biggest bat in the sky, you might be the easiest target. You’re also going to provide a hunter with the most meat,” explained Ruhs.

While other factors could contribute to the trend—such as deforestation and climate change—hunting warrants targeted attention because flying fox meat provides a fair share of the protein for local diets, now showing up on roadside restaurant menus (“hotely”) and even supermarkets.

This, of course, is no good for the flying fox—both in terms of its size and its overall survival. And, since smaller bats constitute smaller ferries for pollen, it also shrinks the role of Madagascan flying foxes in pollination.

Devin Reese is the executive editor of Natural History and a science writer based in Alexandria, Virginia.

Framed by their car’s windshield, and then again by my rearview mirror, a man and a woman who seem to be a couple look like they'd rather be anywhere but together. He’s behind the wheel, doing all the talking; she’s looking straight ahead, motionless like a marble statue. Gradually, her face wears a desperate expression that only grows more hopeless as he continues talking and gesticulating.  

In the supermarket checkout line, I pick up a copy of TIME magazine for the first time in God knows how long, drawn to a painting of Jesus Christ on the cover. It’s a special edition promising to tell us “Who he was. Who he is. His miracles, his mission, his love.” I expect to see a lot of biblical sheep inside, but I don’t find any. I buy the issue as an artifact. I stopped believing in TIME magazine a long time ago. 

Down the street, a place that pretended to be a legitimate art gallery for a couple of months, showing the worst possible commercial art, has finally given up, and now it’s selling fur coats. A man in a cowboy hat walks past two girls dancing for a social media video. The air is chilly, and I think of buying myself a leather jacket.   

She looks at me with the most loving eyes as she holds a stack of perfectly folded laundry. She comforts me with her wide, auspicious smile, her jet-black hair, and her wrinkle-free, porcelain skin. I feel safe, accepted, and not judged. “Fast service, same day,” she promises because she’s just a model in an ad for a laundromat.

—Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief

Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality

“As an adult and as a journalist, I have stared shamelessly.” That refusal to look away is precisely what data journalist, writer, and artist Mona Chalabi has built her deeply principled career on. Known best for her indelible data visualizations, from the obscenity of Jeff Bezos’s wealth to the Israeli government’s starvation of Palestinians in Gaza and the racial and gender biases in museum collections, the Pulitzer Prize-winning Iraqi-British journalist tackles the subject of wealth and economic inequality in America in her first book, Ten Lives: How What We Have Shapes Who We Are (2026). | Lakshmi Rivera Amin

Whether you’re pursuing a degree, developing your professional expertise, or deepening your knowledge of contemporary art, discover opportunities to learn from specialists and engage directly with the international art world.

items.title: Two Centuries After This Bronze Leg Emerged From a Scottish Bog, Archaeologists Believe It May Have Belonged to a Towering Statue of a Roman Emperor on Horseback
items.author: Smithsonian Smart News
items.summary: Long thought to have been looted from northern England by Scottish tribes, the larger-than-life leg may have actually been displayed in Roman Scotland, before it was carefully dismantled and buried by retreating forces

the bronze leg

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In 1820, a larger-than-life gilded bronze lower leg was pulled out of a bog in the Scottish Borders region. For more than two centuries, historians discredited the idea that the Roman-era artifact came from Scotland, instead assuming that it was hacked off a monument in England and hauled north by marauding tribes.

But ahead of “ Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire ,” an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland (NMS), researchers have determined that the so-called “Milsington leg” was not stolen from the south, nor was it violently severed. Instead, they posit that it formed part of a colossal equestrian statue of the Roman Emperor Antoninus Pius that once stood in southern Scotland in the second century C.E., before it was dismantled by retreating Roman troops.

“This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome’s second attempt at conquering Scotland,” Fraser Hunter , principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at NMS, says in a statement .

Roman campaigns into modern-day Scotland began in the 70s C.E., several decades after the conquest of Britain . Emperor Hadrian , who ruled from 117 C.E. to 138 C.E., consolidated the Romans’ northernmost limit in northern England, where Hadrian’s Wall still stands.

Hadrian’s successor, Antoninus Pius, pushed his armies north again, and in the early 140s C.E. fortified a position about 100 miles north of Hadrian’s Wall, known as the Antonine Wall . A few years after Antoninus Pius died in 161 C.E., the Roman armies retreated south, back to Hadrian’s Wall.

The timeline of the second century C.E. Roman invasion of southern Scotland—and eventual withdrawal—provides the context for the bronze limb.

Close inspection reveals that rather than bearing jagged axe or saw marks, the upper edge remains intact, just as Roman metalworkers originally cast it in the 140s C.E. An absence of gilding around the knee indicates that the leg was covered by a tunic or cloak, part of a larger statue, perhaps similar to the equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome

“When you look, you see it hasn’t been hacked off, it’s a complete leg,” Hunter explains to the Telegraph ’s Ruby Cline. “So rather than loot, it looks as if the statue has been carefully decommissioned at the end of its life.”

When Roman forces abandoned southern Scotland, they routinely dismantled and buried prized monuments, including stone altars and inscriptions from the Antonine Wall, rather than leave them behind, per the statement.

Installing a large, visually impressive statue in a border region was purposeful for Antoninus Pius, for whom victory in Scotland was “something which was worth celebrating,” Hunter explains in the statement.

Politically, too, “it makes sense, the Romans producing propaganda right in those contested areas,” Hunter tells the Telegraph . To Scottish Iron Age communities with virtually no tradition of naturalistic human portraiture, a gleaming gilded emperor on horseback would have appeared “really, really alien,” Hunter tells the Guardian ’s Severin Carrell.

Following its excavation in 1820 near Hawick , Scotland, the Milsington leg spent a century tucked away in the Dalkeith Palace , near Edinburgh.

Upon hearing of the discovery, Scottish writer Sir Walter Scott noted in a February 1820 letter to Lord Montagu that finding such a large Roman artifact “in so wild a place, has something very irritating to the curiosity,” adding that he hoped to examine the piece and possibly dig for the remaining fragments himself.

In the exhibition, the Milsington leg is mounted onto a full-scale silhouette reconstruction of horse and rider. The exhibition also features a digital facial reconstruction of a decapitated man buried near the Roman fort of Inveresk , alongside an intricate, tin-coated enamel brooch from Pathhead that may have been a diplomatic gift from Roman forces to a local leader. Other artifacts on view are a unique animal-relief earthenware bowl, the skeleton of a carefully buried cavalry horse and two altars from a temple dedicated to Mithras , a deity of the sun.
