items.cleanReaderHtml:
A village gathering place, jewellery inspired by flowers worn at the ear, woven bamboo furniture and a visual identity created through photography: meet the four Grand Prize winners of the inaugural Design Values Award.

Announced on 27 October 2026, the award’s 20 winners explore how design can give familiar materials, customs and places new possibilities. Launched in 2024 by Design Society in Shenzhen and the V&A in London, the award celebrates contemporary Chinese design, with a focus on sustainable development, cultural dialogue and quality of life.

The four Grand Prize projects explore these ideas through architecture, jewellery, furniture, lighting and graphic design.

In Fengwu Village in eastern China, an old residence known as Yingfengli had disappeared, leaving a small square that offered little protection from the weather. Architecture practice IARA approached the site as both a record of village history and a place with the potential to serve its community.

Built over the foundations of the former house, FW JI· The Rural Memory Museum uses local materials to connect the new structure with its surroundings. Its covered communal space provides a sheltered gathering place for villagers, allowing the traces of a former home to shape a new public space.

The jury recognised the project’s sensitive approach to collective memory and its creation of a covered communal space that supports village life.

The Dai custom of women adorning their ears with flowers is the starting point for Zhang Yu’s Whisper. Using aluminium, brass and polycarbonate, Zhang translates this form of adornment into contemporary jewellery.

His practice is grounded in field research into the cultures and crafts of Yunnan, with a particular focus on Dai traditions. Whisper draws attention to the custom and the cultural knowledge it carries, translating a tradition that the designer describes as fading into contemporary jewellery.

The jury recognised the work’s striking visual impact, material innovation and craftsmanship, and its sensitive contemporary interpretation of Dai cultural heritage.

Bamboo has been central to Mingyu Xu’s practice since 2016. For Motuo Bamboo Forest, he draws on the Menba bamboo-weaving tradition of Motuo in Tibet, applying it to a modular collection of furniture and lighting.

Pendant lamps, stools, coffee tables and floor lamps extend the possibilities of the woven material across a range of domestic objects. Xu, who founded MINGYU XU STUDIO in London, explores how traditional weaving skills can find new applications in contemporary design.

The jury celebrated the collection’s experimental use of bamboo, its sustainability potential and the strength of its lighting designs.

For the visual identity of the 2024 Jin Daiqiang Design Award, Shenzhen-based graphic designer Liao Bofeng took inspiration from The Crow and the Water. In this fable, a thirsty crow drops stones into a vessel until the water rises within reach.

Liao explored the story’s theme of ingenuity through a handmade installation, which he photographed to create the graphics. By constructing and photographing physical objects, he examines the creative possibilities of simple materials and questions designers’ dependence on digital tools. The resulting identity makes physical experimentation central to the finished graphics.

In the V&A/RCA History of Design MA programme, our students have the opportunity to contribute to the day-to-day running of the museum. They can do this through placement projects or by assisting with events. In this post, 2026 graduate Elizabeth (Xinyi) He shares her experience at the National Art Library Discovery Day, where she spoke to visitors about a book that lies at the very roots of the V&A’s history and her own MA research.

Each year, the National Art Library holds four Discovery Days, during which V&A members of staff present and talk to visitors about hidden-gem books and other items in the collection. For the Discovery Day held on 10 April 2026, History of Design master’s students from the joint postgraduate programme between the Victoria and Albert Museum and the Royal College of Art were invited to select an item related to one of the featured themes: Botany, Fashion and the Great Exhibition of 1851

As one of the participating students, I chose Dickinsons’ comprehensive pictures of the Great Exhibition of 1851 . A book made up of detailed coloured plates, it’s almost like visually eavesdropping on the Great Exhibition. I knew the book well because I had studied it for my MA dissertation titled ‘Cole, Arnoux and Minton’s 1851 Journey: Looking for British Identity in Pottery’, which developed from a placement I undertook with the Acting Head of Programme Dr Simona Valeriani on the ‘Henry Cole’s Diaries Project’ .

While studying Henry Cole’s travel journals, I came across Dickinson’s book. You may wonder how Dickinson’s book and Henry Cole are connected. Well, as you may have read elsewhere, Henry Cole was the organiser of the Great Exhibition, the ‘first world fair’, which undoubtedly influenced his later collecting interests and travelling destinations.

Dickinsons’ Comprehensive Pictures of the Great Exhibition of 1851 consisted of a series of lithographs which reproduced original watercolours made by the artists Joseph Nash (1809–1878), Louis Haghe (1806–1885), and David Roberts (1796–1864) for Prince Albert. Each illustration visually described a different national pavilion. In what follows, I will discuss how the book’s illustrations and commentary show how the Exhibition was a catalyst for innovation and competition through the examples of the French and German pavilions. The history presented in this Great Exhibition demonstrates international investment in industrial progress. This interests us all because, although technology has changed dramatically since then, the agenda of supporting scientific innovation remains quite relevant.

The Sèvres Court at the French pavilion was a hotspot. Although Chinese porcelain had long served as the historical and technological foundation for European porcelain production, the British juries at the Great Exhibition paid more attention to French porcelain as both a commercial rival and an artistic model for British manufacture. Unsurprisingly, the book included a full-length page devoted to the Sèvres Court and the Department of Practical Art which collected French porcelains for teaching purposes.

The fixation with foreign porcelain and pottery was real. Henry Cole and Richard Redgrave (the V&A’s first art superintendent) voiced their concerns when they admitted in the Journal of Design (1850) that ‘the best of the pottery designs [were] imitations of the old Dresden and Sèvres designs.’ English manufacturers needed to develop a more distinctive identity. Manufacturers such as Minton and Wedgwood did the trick when they came up with a new (and affordable!) type of earthenware in the style of maiolica. Mass-produced and competitively priced, their products appealed to socially aspirational markets, including in the United States.

But, besides the French, there were the Germans or, better said, the manufacturers form the German Customs Union, made of twenty-six Germanic States including Prussia, Bavaria, and Saxony. Their bronzes and woodcarving were perceived to be of ‘a superior taste in design, composition, and ornamentation’ than the English. Not only that, their products combined ‘utility, taste, and cheapness’. German industry was considered ‘in a satisfactory state of progress.’ Beyond the practical arts, its displays of mining and metallurgy demonstrated exceptional scientific ability. This admiration was not merely aesthetic; it sought to stimulate British industrial progress. Dickinsons’ Comprehensive Pictures of the Great Exhibition of 1851 visually amplified that.

The MA in History of Design provided me with the skills to identify and explore the connections between science and art, which I further developed and applied during my placement on the Henry Cole’s Diaries Project. When I learnt that the National Art Library Discovery Day would focus on the Great Exhibition of 1851, I quickly signed up for the opportunity to share my passion for the subject with museum visitors. The colourful plates in Dickinsons’ Comprehensive Pictures of the Great Exhibition of 1851 are a visually immersive vehicle for exploring this historical event and the debates surrounding it.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

Science is often characterized as moving in slow motion, with experiments yielding small incremental steps. However, as information is shared and knowledge coalesces, multiple scientists can converge on a “eureka” moment nearly simultaneously. So who gets the credit for the big discoveries and who becomes the footnote? How do you prove who was first?

Charles Darwin (1809–1882), like many of his contemporaries, was a voracious correspondent with other scientists. These scientists shared thoughts and ideas via letters over many years as theories were debated and refined. Darwin’s correspondence with Harvard botanist Asa Gray (1810–1888), particularly a September 5, 1857 letter and enclosure from Darwin that is held at the Harvard University Botany Libraries and available in BHL, would prove vital in demonstrating Darwin’s priority for the theory of evolution over fellow Englishman Alfred Russel Wallace (1823–1913).

Left: Asa Gray, c. 1865–1867. Unique ID 0946. Right: Charles Darwin, 1861. Unique IDs DC04, 0074, 0089. Both images from the Botany Libraries photograph collection, circa 1770–2020. gra00083. Botany Libraries, Harvard University.

In the mid-1850s, scientists were struggling with questions related to the origin and distribution of species and their variations. The great explorations around the world, coupled with modern classification systems, provided a wealth of data to evaluate and debate prevailing theories. Particularly difficult to explain were geographically isolated species and widespread but geographically disjointed species. So what was the “origin of species”?

In 1854, Charles Darwin was contemplating several components of the “origin” question. Darwin’s extensive work on barnacles, summarized in A monograph on the sub-class Cirripedia, with figures of all the species , demonstrated that a large amount of variation existed that was not well explained by a popular theory that life emerged from a single location on Earth.

Intrigued by Gray’s insights into Flora Novae-Zelandiae that Joseph Dalton Hooker (1817–1911) shared with him, Darwin contacted Gray directly on April 25, 1855 with questions about alpine flora species and distributions outlined in Gray’s Manual of the Botany of the Northern United States (see also Darwin’s annotated copy of the 1856 2nd edition). Thus began a years-long correspondence that expanded from data requests to philosophical discussions and influenced Darwin’s theory of evolution.

After three years of correspondence, Darwin shared with Gray in a July 20, 1857, letter :

“Nineteen years (!) ago it occurred to me that whilst attention employed on Natural History I might perhaps do good if I noted any sort of facts bearing on the question on the origin of species; and this I have since been doing. Either species have been independently created, or they have descended from other species, like varieties from one species… I must tell you that I have come to the relentless conclusion that there are no such things as independently created species, the species are only strongly defined varieties.”

Gray responded in August 1857 (complete letter not available), and Darwin followed up with the September 5, 1857 , letter that included an enclosure with his six-points establishing the theory of evolution by natural selection.

Charles Darwin letter to Asa Gray, September 5, 1857 . Asa Gray correspondence files of the Gray Herbarium, 1820–1931. gra00078. Botany Libraries, Harvard University.

With his theory still unpublished but documented in correspondence, Darwin received a package on June 18, 1858, from Alfred Russel Wallace expressing similar theories. In a letter dated July 4, 1858 , Darwin asked Gray to confirm his receipt of the September 5, 1857 letter and enclosure to establish his priority for the theory of evolution by natural selection .

The “ Darwin-Wallace paper ” was published in 1858 by the Linnean Society with the assistance of Joseph Dalton Hooker and Charles Lyell. The paper contains three items:

“In June 1842 I first allowed myself the satisfaction of writing a very brief abstract of my theory in pencil in 34 pages and this was enlarged during the summer of 1844 into one of 230 pages, which I had fairly copied out and still possess.”

items.author: The Public Domain Review
items.summary: A neopagan visual archive meant to rival the iconic power of the Christian West.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
A nude lies upon an open tome, bloodied branch in hand. With a skull for a face, but otherwise enfleshed, the body bisects Art Nouveau illustrations: a red-haired woman circled by some kind of serpent and a colder image, whose face is obscured by a forest of hair. Is this the same woman, present, past, and further past? A memento mori of a kind? And how should we interpret the title, Old Truth Lies in Books ( Stara prawda w księgach leży )? Painted in 1910 by Marian Wawrzeniecki, the image seems to gesture toward something menacing and mythical, forgotten by history but alluded to in antiquities and the pages of artbooks.

For all of his later Symbolist leanings, Wawrzeniecki was trained in Kraków, in the academic style of Polish history painting. The style was large-format and maximalist, mixing subjects from Polish history with allegorical tableaux. From Antonín Dvořák’s Slavonic Dances to Jan Matejko’s masterpieces, high art and folk forms blended to create local senses of cultural identity distinct from the empires and colonial powers of occidental Europe. Yet Wawrzeniecki surpassed this cultural era of Romantic nationalism by reaching further into the past than his peers and masters could have imagined.

Although he was, by any measure, a minor painter, Wawrzeniecki was a majorly influential archaeologist, discovering not only the first obsidian artifacts on Polish lands but also early earthen shelters, ceramics, and steles. His pioneering work left its mark on his visual art, including one of the earliest paintings depicting an archaeological excavation. Rozkopany kurhan (“The Excavated Burial Mound”), painted between 1891 and 1892, is notable for how it takes up the conventions of history painting to depict not an idealized scene from the past, but rather the gulf separating those discovering prehistory from the fragmentary, quizzical remains of this long-ago time.

The archaeologist’s task necessarily involves applying the imagination to interpret their findings, but Wawrzeniecki’s ran wild. He began to see his region’s pagan prehistory as its true essence, finding a radical rupture between this paradise and the Christianized fallen world that had supplanted it. His artistic output was colored by his archaeological research to such an extent that by the 1910s and 1920s, he mostly produced colored illustrations of pagan Slavic rituals.

In several, female nudes are tied to a tree, or strung up between two pillars. A basilisk often lurks nearby, sometimes smiling creepily. These women became an idée fixe, populating more and more of his later illustrations, the style of which abandons his academic training in oil painting for the bright colors of textbook illustrations. It would be easy to conflate these plump and faceless female nudes with pulp erotica — and similar accusations were already leveled at the artist in his lifetime. But Wawrzeniecki’s allegorical tableaux, painted at the turn of the twentieth century, offer up the possibility of a less reductive reading.

Marian Wawrzeniecki, A Fairy Tale About a Princess and a Dragon , ca. 1904–1908

Read as symbolic vehicles, these neopagan nudes become multilayered allegories: for an elusive pagan-Slavic essence, for creative devotion, for artworks packaged and assessed by critics. Their hostility to his cultural theories, and Wawrzeniecki’s pugnacious disposition, led him to publish numerous ethnographic studies, defenses of history painting, takedowns of the younger generation of Symbolist painters, and open letters to his critics from the 1910s onward. He came to see Gothic architecture and Renaissance painting as Germanic and Italic aberrations: successive regimes of a thousand-year-long cultural colonization of pagan Slavdom by Christianity.

How to reconcile Wawrzeniecki’s elegant early paintings with the plethora of designs and storybook illustrations he produced for the last three decades of his career? Torn between archaeology and oil painting, his intellect evolved in an obsessive direction, collecting and producing a neopagan visual archive to rival the iconic power of the Christian West. It’s no surprise that conventional markers of quality and professional success became unimportant to him. Even if he never achieved escape velocity, his visual language paved the way for later artists who took up the task. His artistic descendants include Polish-American Stanisław Szukalski (1893–1987), whose neopagan experimental style is the subject of a spectacular 2018 documentary , and his speculative cultural theories found new life in Maria Janion’s pivotal 2006 book Niesamowita Słowiańszczyzna ( Uncanny Slavdom ), which argues that Polish culture’s perennial obsession with ghosts, monsters, and phantoms proves that this pagan past never really stopped haunting the art and poetry created since. Perhaps it never will.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Eleven young photographers reflect on the times we live in to share these original photographs.

A Moment in Time is a body of work exploring the now; what sense or feeling this moment brings, and how might we capture this for the future.

Working with the V&A South Kensington’s Learning team and creatives Michael Akuagwu (multi-media based artist and designer) and Jude Amponsah (Graphic Designer, Photographer and Filmmaker), the group developed their practice through a five day programme in August 2026.

Through research within the V&A South Kensington, the group took inspiration from Photography Now, The Photography Centre’s Contemporary display. Working collaboratively, they pushed their practice, skills and knowledge; developing their craft as a collective and creating individual and original new work.

‘I have developed technically and grown more in generating ideas and concepts’

Emerging themes included nostalgia and memory, development of the self through human form, movement, and queerness. Creatives also explored how we visually define our generation through fashion and youth culture, how we carry our culture and how our heritage shapes us.

Each photographer was already creating inspiring work, but this week provided a dedicated space for creatives to deepen their practice and explore new possibilities, offering the opportunity to develop skills, share perspectives and present ideas.

‘I gained confidence in articulating my artistic approach’

Guests included Photographer Anais Stupka , and museum staff Isaac Huxtable (Assistant Curator, Photography) and Rachel Flaxman (Interpretation Producer). This programme was brought together by the V&A Young People’s Programme Team and supported throughout by Wen Sheng-Hong and Jasprit Singh.

This work will be on show at the V&A South Kensington on 22 January 2027 during Make and Meet, an evening event for young artists to connect and create at V&A South Kensington.

To find out more about programmes young creatives can get involved in, visit Young people

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Museum seating is often invisible. The public only notices a seat, or its absence, when a seat is needed. And museums prioritise, as expected, the visitor’s experience and the collections’ preservation and display, dealing with seating mostly as an accessibility requirement.

However, as design historian Judy Attfield would say, museum seats belong to the museum’s ‘material culture of everyday life’. By understanding museum seating as material culture, disciplines such as design history may unveil unknown stories belonging to the wider life of museums.

At the V&A, the so-called ‘historic benches’, some of them in use for more than 150 years, hide surprisingly rich accounts on how the museum shaped ways of viewing and experiencing the collection.

Looking for a place to sit, a visitor arriving at the V&A’s Cast Courts today might find several long, wooden benches, effaced and discoloured at the edges, but elegantly finished with carved finials. The visitor probably does not know that some of these benches have seen the turning of two centuries, two world wars, and everything else that has happened since the 1850s. Some of them have likely been in use since the day the South Kensington Museum (SKM), which preceded the V&A, first opened.

The wooden benches, informally called ‘historic benches’ by V&A’s staff, appeared in several images from the 1860s portraying the SKM, as pictured above. Many were made by Johnstone & Jeanes, a Victorian cabinetmaker and upholsterer. The name shifted several times due to changes in ownership, but the firm was active under ‘Johnstone & Jeanes’ between 1840 and 1882, placing some of the V&A’s benches within that period.

Johnstone & Jeanes was known for innovative designs and elegant furniture. The maker’s famous Jupe expandable table attracted attention in the 1851 Exhibition. Many pieces won international prizes. The company was employed by Queen Victoria and manufactured furniture designed by Prince Albert for Buckingham Palace, as well as the well-known Lawrence Alma-Tadema’s designs for Henry Gurdon Marquand’s Music Room in New York. The firm also supplied display cases for the SKM and the museum’s director chair, which was probably used by Henry Cole, pictured below. The stock of surviving Johnstone & Jeanes furniture is believed to be low, increasing the historical importance of the V&A’s benches.

The wooden benches were placed in different galleries in the SKM, such as in the ‘Raphael Room’ as shown below. This gallery housed the Raphael Cartoons, the famous set of 16th-century paintings on paper by Raphael that served as designs for the tapestries hung in the Sistine Chapel. Balancing the Cartoons between the realms of art and design, the museum has shaped different ways of seeing and experiencing their dual nature through changes in galleries, displays and furniture. The historic benches, following a script of simplicity that contrasted with SKM’s highly embellished architecture, assumed a relevant role in that discourse that reads from the design of the bench itself.

The use of thin strips of wood within a functional design provided minimal visual interference with the display. Unlike the comfortable, domesticised ottomans of Louvre’s Salon Carré , from where flaneurs and ladies could languidly admire art, these were seats to teach the public about design, placed in a museum built for learning. Furthermore, their vaguely reminiscence of park benches or church pews conveyed a message of universality. Alongside free entrance and evening opening hours, the SKM’s benches were a silent agent in providing access for all, which was also probably understood as requiring sturdy and solid seats capable of surviving a less selective audience.

Their functionality, however, stopped at the finials that punctuated their backs, which revealed traces of the typically Victorian combination of styles and passion for ornament. The finials acted as a quiet surrender to decoration, a proof that these benches were still a product of their own time.

In the absence of detailed archives about the commission and purchase of these pieces of furniture, the V&A’s benches provide the design historian with a part of the museum’s past that has not been materialised into words. Moreover, these benches were literally hiding underneath the wooden boards details about their history that would be otherwise unknown. It was only after turning the benches upside down and examining the underside of each bench with a smartphone’s torch, outside opening hours, that I found faded engraved marks from Johnstone & Jeanes. These marks allowed me to date some of the benches and to bring new stories to the fore. Design history guides the historian into reading objects, extracting their messages, and into placing them alongside the wider context in which they exist.

This post stems from Joana’s MA dissertation, completed in the V&A/RCA’s MA History of Design programme in 2021, entitled ‘De-scribing Museum Seats: Design and Art in the V&A’s Raphael Cartoons Galleries’. The examination of museum benches was kindly authorised and supervised by V&A staff.

Joana continued her studies in the V&A/RCA’s History of Design programme. She completed a PhD in 2026, working at the encounter between design history and sound studies. Her PhD thesis is entitled ‘There’s Somebody at the Door: a History of British Domesticity Through the Sound and Material Culture of Friedland Doorbells, 1930s-2010s’.

Joana Albernaz Delgado is a design historian and researcher devoted to mixed-media methodologies. A former lawyer, Joana graduated from the History of Design MA Programme at the Victoria and Albert...

I never paid much attention to museum benches until I visited the V&A with my aunt, who needed regular breaks between galleries. We ended up noticing the carved details on the seats almost as much as the exhibits. A few weeks later, I was hunting for a similar wooden bench for our hallway and spent an evening reading wayfair reviews about comfort and durability. It made me realize that seating can be beautiful, practical, and part of a place’s story all at once. I love that this project treats those overlooked benches as design objects worth studying much more closely.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Halloween may be over, but Spooky Season is alive and well. To celebrate, we are highlighting some of the terrifying treasures that sit within the National Art Library collections at V&A East Storehouse.

With around 300,000 library books held at Storehouse, spanning theatre and performance, local history and British topography, and historic children’s books, there is no shortage of weird and wonderful publications.

The seven titles listed here represent just a few frightful favourites, all available to view in the Storehouse Study Centre.

It stands to reason that a city as old and as large as London would have seen its fair share of burial grounds and high-profile funerals. This guide highlights some of the most famous graves across the City of London and beyond. From London’s ‘magnificent seven,’ the large garden cemeteries built by the Victorians to alleviate crowding and unsafe burial grounds, to medieval churchyards, the book maps the burial places of kings, queens, pickpockets, artists and more.

Karl Marx, William Blake, George Eliot and V&A’s very own Henry Cole are just a few of the illustrious graves to be found in this book. What better way to spend Halloween weekend than strolling amongst the tombs of London’s historic graveyards?

It would be fair to say that Sarah Bernhardt was comfortable with the idea of her own mortality – as a tragedienne, she was used to dying in front of an audience night after night. But she was also known for keeping a satin lined coffin in her bedroom, which she often slept in, lay in whilst preparing her roles, and posed for photographs in, contributing to her dramatic image.

Sarah Bernhardt was one the most famous French stage actresses of the late 19 th and early 20 th centuries – so it isn’t surprising that when she passed away in 1923 aged 78, a crowd of 30,000 mourners attended her funeral, and accompanied her casket across Paris to the Père Lachaise Cemetery, stopping off at the Sarah Bernhardt Theatre along the way.

This scrapbook, compiled by an unknown fan, collects obituaries and articles documenting her incredible life and career as well as her elaborate funeral, which included extravagant floral arrangements, black plumed horses to pull her cortege, and an accompanying entourage of mourners.

This pocket-sized book of emblems is jam packed full of skeletons! These skeletal images are reproductions of Hans Holbein’s Dance of Death (first published 1538). The Dance of Death or Danse Macabre was a popular allegorical genre from the late Middle Ages, where a personification of Death, in the form of a skeleton, invites representatives from all walks of life into a dance to the grave. They were produced as memento mori , or reminders of the reader’s own mortality- whatever your position in society, death was the great leveler.

These reproductions were made by John Bewick, a wood engraver active in the 18 th century. His brother, Thomas Bewick, was widely credited as being a pioneer of wood engraving, his fine lines and the naturalism of his animal prints in works such as A history of British birds earning him widespread popularity. John Bewick was apprenticed to him before forging his own career as an engraver, predominantly working on children’s books. Sadly, he passed away at the age of 35, before he was able to establish his own reputation as an artist and engraver.

Haven’t we all had moments where our imagination gets the better of us in the dark? The Fakenham ghost tells an eerie tale of walking home at night through the Norfolk countryside, and of being followed by an unseen, possibly malevolent presence… Though initially frightening, Robert Bloomfield’s poem masterfully balances tension and humour, and the accompanying unsigned prints also reflect this in their interplay of darkness and light. Though eerie, the illustrations also hint very early on at what, or who, the ‘ghost’ may be…perhaps a small donkey?

Robert Bloomfield was a self-taught poet and cobbler from Suffolk, whose poetry about rural life met with great praise during his lifetime. The Fakenham ghost was originally published as part of his poetry collection Rural Tales in 1802. This 1806 edition was published by William Darton, who specialized in children’s books.

The 19 th century saw a rise in Spiritualism – the belief that the living can commune with the dead, usually through mediums or seances. J. H. Brown, the author of Spectropia , was not so taken with this belief, and in 1864 set out to prove that ghost sightings were nothing more than an optical illusion.

Following an introduction condemning the “absurd follies” of Spiritualism, this book presents 16 lithographed plates—13 hand‑coloured—designed to produce vivid afterimage illusions.

items.title: A Cult Grew Around the First Emperor of Rome in 27 B.C. A New Book Argues His Followers Might Have Created the Template for Christianity
items.author: Smithsonian Arts & Culture
items.summary: Augustus was seen as a descendant of the gods who would go on to redefine authority. New research posits that his rule paved the way for Jesus

items.cleanReaderHtml:
How did the scattered followers of an itinerant preacher come to form the most populous religion in the world? Tim Whitmarsh—a classicist at the University of Cambridge and author of magisterial books about empire, the early novel and more—offers a compelling answer in his new book, Rome’s Age of Revolution: Augustus, Empire and the Making of Christianity. To wit, Christianity took much of its shape from the cult of Augustus, first emperor of Rome.

The Augustan age saw a unique revolution that redefined authority, space and literature, remaking both the inner world and the outer. Augustus drew on centuries-old Roman prophecies to cast himself as the promised one . According to his propaganda, Italy experienced auguries and miracles at Augustus’ nativity; Augustus was declared a descendant of Rome’s mythical founder, Aeneas, and therefore of the gods, and he promised to renew Roman liberty from the decadence of the late Republic. As Whitmarsh writes: “The new world was presented as the fulfillment of all the best ideals of the old.” Just so, Jesus’s birth was claimed as the fulfillment of Old Testament prophecies about a coming emissary of God on Earth, and this novel form of monotheism was simultaneously cast as the fruition of the Hebrew faith.

Whitmarsh goes further, arguing: “What we call messianism is a symbolic byproduct of the concentration of absolute power over vast territories and multiple populations in the hands of one individual or family.” Jesus, then, is “the divine doppelgänger of the most powerful human authority imaginable,” i.e., Augustus, and Christianity came to operate “as a strange doppelgänger of the Roman imperial system.”

Just as unitary empire helped prepare people for the concept of a unitary god, Augustan infrastructure—including an empire-spanning network of roads—literally paved the way for the transmission of stories about Jesus and his followers. Letters and trade flourished, and religions, which had long been deeply tied to location, could become universal.

Whitmarsh has a keen eye for the religio-cultural give-and-take between Judea and Rome: “The Christian idea of a savior king ... is partially shaped by the prior model of Augustus as a world savior. But that model was itself partially indebted to Jewish messianic traditions.” Causality, after all, is a subtle thing, and Whitmarsh avoids oversimplifications. He invokes a cultural dynamic that he calls a “swirl,” which gets kicked up by political or technological revolution—but also precedes the revolution. It can be a hazy concept. But with Whitmarsh’s sharp and often inspired readings of history and literature, it offers an imprecise but necessary honesty. Thou shalt not bear false witness, indeed.

Augustus relied on poets like Virgil, the famed bard of the early Roman Empire, to popularize his reign.

Virgil’s eclogues, a series of 10 pastoral poems, describe a savior child born to a virgin mother. The poem is dated to 40 B.C.E. and has been interpreted by some as a prophecy of Christ.

Virgil wrote that the Earth would celebrate the savior’s birth with miracles: Snakes would die, and goats would no longer fear lions.

The poem’s vision is referred to as the Cumaean Prophecy—and itself may have been inspired by earlier sources, possibly the eastern cult of Mithras, or from the book of Isaiah.

Tim Whitmarsh draws parallels that suggest the Roman Empire may have helped shape Christianity

This article is a selection from the November 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine

items.cleanReaderHtml:
When the Bristol Channel flooded in 1607, it was not just one of the worst natural disasters in British history, it was also a sign, for many, that they had strayed from the path of God. Erik Crnkovich examines the overlap of miraculous weather and the early modern printing industry, which cultivated a thirst for all things occult, exotic, and odd.

Title-page woodcut from 1607, A True Report of Certaine Wonderfull Ouerflowings of Waters, Now Lately in Summerset-shire, Norfolke, and Other Places of England (1607) — Source .

When the Bristol Channel flooded on January 30, 1607, pamphlets describing it as God’s warning to a wayward people likewise flooded out of London’s booming presses. Rare weather events of all sorts are ironically commonplace in seventeenth-century news — a century otherwise tempestuous in its frequent, often literal, chopping and changing in church and state. In fact, the two are reflections of each other. True, British weather was consistently inconsistent during the Little Ice Age, a period of prolonged cold and wet that would not end for another two centuries. But the headlines reporting “prodigious” thunderstorms, “miraculous” apparitions, and “terrible” earthquakes were often followed by interpretations of them as moral weathervanes — divine providence, a sign to repent and return to the proverbial straight and narrow.

It is perhaps little surprise, then, that the pamphleteer William Jones rushed to the presses when a storm surge inundated 518 square kilometres surrounding the Bristol Channel. Present scholarship counts 2,000 recorded deaths, making it one of Britain’s worst natural disasters and, according to Jones, a judgement from God. 1

Like many disaster narratives, Jones starts his account with the truism that the morning of the flood was just like any other: the skies were clear and sunny, ploughmen cut their furrows, shepherds led their flocks to pasture, farmers set about their morning rounds in the yards when, suddenly, “mighty Hills of water” appeared on the horizon, “tumbling one over another”. 3 The waters swept away buildings and bridges, inundated granaries and warehouses, and flooded the streets of Bristol; across the countryside, the carcasses of wild animals, drowned cattle, sheep, chickens, and (oddly) ducks dotted the flood waters. Some people managed to flee, some drowned; others sought refuge in trees and church steeples where they endured hunger and cold for days before rescue.

Title-page woodcut from Gods Warning to His People of England (1607) — Source .

A Protestant, Jones lays some of the blame on the “late Papistical Conspiracy of Traitors”, but the sinfulness is generally all-encompassing. 4 This is less than surprising. The weight of morality in England was more immediate after the Reformation: clerical and saintly intermediaries between Creator and creation had been removed, innate sinfulness emphasised, and God positioned as a strict schoolmaster meting out punishment and reward. While prodigious events were acknowledged as natural, therefore, they were still thought of as induced by human immorality. Pamphleteers routinely draw on cardinal transgressions, such as adultery and blasphemy, but also charge specific places with specific penchants (Cork, usury; Tiverton, miserliness; Banbury, breaking the Sabbath). This waywardness required God to intervene, to exercise “special” providence to steer humankind along the path of “general” providence, the predetermined course set in stone at creation. Natural phenomena were often interpreted as signs of divine intervention in seventeenth-century print, particularly when preternatural in effect and prodigious in scale. 5

Jones emphasises the flood’s apocalyptically topsy-turvy nature: the land is turned to water, the rich are made poor, the fertile is laden with salt, and scholars are left dumbfounded. Yet the “merciless” waters also provide a stage for miraculous, divine acts of mercy. In Monmouthshire, a milkmaid stranded on a high bank is eventually saved, “through God’s good help”, when some large troughs are lashed together and two muscly men punt to the rescue. 6 Moreover, Jones asks us to “mark what befell, at this time, of the strangeness of other creatures”: because, as the tide rose around the bank, the milkmaid found her haven “also covered over, with wild beasts” — dogs, cats, foxes, and rodents — “that thither to seek for succour” and yet, predator and prey mingled, “in this danger of life, they not once offered to express their natural envy: But in a gentle sort, they freely enjoyed the liberty of life.” 7

In a different account of the flood, A True Report of Certain Wonderful Overflowings of Water (1607), an anonymous author illustrates the miraculous with “tragi-comical” stories that are more eyebrow-raising than hair-raising. The author reports, for instance, that a man planning to travel to a local town to “be merry” had his horse saddled and at the ready when “the wind came about, the point of his compass was changed, his voyage by land was to be made by water, or else not at all.” Instead of fleeing on horseback (as some do in Jones’ account), the man abandons his steed and retreats up his roof, sitting “astride” its ridge. The anonymous author then gleefully describes how the roof is lifted off the house by the flood and begins to float — so “Neptune” could see “how well he could ride” — eventually, lo and behold, taking him to “the very town, where in the morning he meant to take up his inn.” 8

Title-page from A True Report of Certain Wonderful Overflowings (1607) — Source .

Title-page from Lamentable Newes Out of Monmouthshire (1607) — Source .

It is difficult to know how much credence a contemporary reader placed in these reports. But that there was wariness of spurious news is evidenced, if anything, by the lengths to which their writers went to assert their credibility. Some are, granted, no more than lip service: the author of the “tragi-comical” accounts above simply says they include “none but those that are true”. 9 While a third account of the Bristol flood, entitled Lamentable Newes Out of Monmouthshire (1607), makes a more concerted effort, the author saying they initially refused to write on the disaster because “of the usual unfaithfulness of men ordinarily in reporting of such accidents”. 10 More strident authors list the names and addresses of eyewitnesses. To prove his account of a miraculous rain shower of wheat, the author William Averell lists, among others, a clothier “Master William Geffreyes dwelling in Ipswich” and “John Bull, servant to Justice Germaye”. 11 A True Relation of the Wonderful Apparition of a Cross in the Moon name-drops none other than the Lord Chancellor of Ireland. 12 Generally, the higher up the social ladder a witness was, the more credible they were thought to be.

The pamphlets were immensely popular, questions about their veracity notwithstanding. Overall, the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries witnessed an “early modern vogue for the preternatural”, to quote historian of science Lorraine Daston, a passion for anything whiffing of oddities, the occult, witchcraft, or exotic news from beyond the horizon. 13 The skies above Britain were no different. This fascination was partly academic: unusual natural phenomena of all sorts stood out in the prevailing scientific paradigm of Francis Bacon as providing a better window into the natural world than simply observing its smooth, quotidian ticking over. But there was also a millenarian culture of moral crisis — tensions between Catholics and Protestants, Roundheads and Cavaliers, Puritans and everyone — that left the public searching for omens. The apogee of the pamphlet and broadside, “true” and “certain” reports of marvels, wonders, and prodigies of all sorts flooded the market, sold from shops around St Paul’s Cathedral, London, huckstered outside of theatres and alehouses, or carried by peddlers into the countryside. 14

Print seller depicted in Marcellus Laroon’s Cryes of the City of London Drawne after the Life (1688) — Source .

items.title: How Astronomers and Art Historians Are Working Together to Identify the Inspiration Behind Famous Works of Art
items.author: Smithsonian Arts & Culture
items.summary: Researchers study paintings and literature to uncover untold history of the works, sometimes finding themselves trying to discern celestial bodies from dust

The Evening Star
Cover image of the Smithsonian Magazine November 2026 issue
Prof. Don Olson
Claude Monet’s Impression, Sunrise
Friedrich

items.cleanReaderHtml:
In the spring of 2025, I fell into some art detective work. My mission was to go to New York’s Metropolitan Museum of Art and get close to The Evening Star by the German Romantic painter Caspar David Friedrich . The Evening Star —a nickname for Venus —joined several works not previously displayed in the United States, part of a Friedrich exhibition called “The Soul of Nature,” honoring the 250th anniversary of the artist’s birth. According to the museum’s description, Venus could be seen as “a tiny bright dot” barely visible above a cloud bank. In the painting, three figures stand on a hill outside Dresden, Germany, at sunset. A young boy at center, his back to the viewer, lifts his arms in exultation. But where was the star? The work’s title character seemed to be missing from prints and art books depicting The Evening Star.

As a caver, I’m normally trying to solve mysteries deep in the earth. This unaccustomed aboveground task came to me, indirectly, from Don Olson , the astronomer and astrophysicist. In 2024, I’d casually met one of his research collaborators, Ava Pope , through her partner, Mike Newsome, both fellow caving enthusiasts. (The two often sponsored caver gatherings at their Virginia farm.) When Pope saw on social media that my wife, Kathy, and I were in New York for the weekend, she texted me. The exhibition would end in less than two months, and she explained that if I could find and photograph Venus, my images might help Olson unravel several mysteries: From what physical spot did Friedrich observe the scene? On what date? And who, for that matter, is the family depicted in the scene? I was determined to find out.

As I would learn, Olson and his students and collaborators have taken on a singular approach, finding new truths in paintings we thought we knew.

Olson began using astronomy to investigate creative works in the 1980s at Texas State University, when an English professor asked him for help understanding complex astronomical passages in “The Franklin’s Tale,” one of Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales . His astronomical research connected an abnormally high tide on the coast of Brittany—a major plot device in the story—to an extreme flood on December 19, 1340, which may have inspired the incident in Chaucer. Besides co-writing a paper about the various lines of evidence that led him to that date, Olson studied astronomical elements in a variety of other works: Claude Monet’s The Cliff, Étretat, Sunset (pinpointing the beach location where the artist stood); Vincent van Gogh’s White House at Night (the golden disk in the sky must be Venus around a sunset in June 1890, as opposed to sunrise, moonrise or moonset); Ansel Adams’ Autumn Moon (the remote and never-before-identified Yosemite location from which the photograph must have been taken); William Shakespeare’s Hamlet (whether the star in the opening scene is a planet, or Tycho’s supernova , or something else); Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein (verifying that the “waking dream” she later described as inspiring her story happened on a moonlit evening in Switzerland on June 16, 1816); and historical events from ancient Rome (locating Julius Caesar’s first invasion of Britain ) to World War II (explaining a disastrous tide for Marines landing at Tarawa in the Central Pacific). Olson realized that many dates and locations where artworks were made, even the very scenes they depicted, had been incorrectly reported in books and exhibitions, which often gave conflicting years and places. Olson felt certain these were errors he could fix by combining astronomical data with site visits and deep dives into historical records.

This article is a selection from the November 2026 issue of Smithsonian magazine

A lanky figure who often wears blue jeans and a Texas State shirt, Olson has long softened his exacting attention to detail with lectures that feature such examples, to make science less “terrifying” to his students. In basic physics classes, he has cast rainbows across the room to explain refraction; in honors-program classes, he has taken undergraduates to Yosemite, Switzerland and other far-flung locations, immersing them in unforgettable fieldwork.

In 2008, Pope, then an undergraduate physics major, took an honors course with Olson titled “Astronomy in Art, History and Literature.” The class changed her life. She partnered with students from other disciplines, she says, using their separate skill sets to find novel solutions to various mysteries. Pope’s first project was to find the dates when one could photograph sunset through a particular V-shaped geological formation in Big Bend National Park in southwest Texas. Olson gave her a puzzle to solve, and she was hooked.

Later in the semester, Olson handed Pope a print of Starry Night —the somewhat more realistic painting by Edvard Munch rather than the more famous one by van Gogh. He asked her to figure out when it was painted. Pope dove into the Munch assignment, calculating astronomical data for the Norwegian resort town of Asgardstrand, where Munch made the painting, a place she’d never visited. Most of the available information about the town’s history was printed in Norwegian, including an archived article from the newspaper Morgenbladet . It confirmed that Munch’s Starry Night had been cataloged in an early exhibition under another name, Abendstern , which, oddly enough, translates to “Evening Star.” Finding this alternate name clarified references to the painting in other historical documents, as well as in Munch’s own hand. It depicted an early evening scene. Importantly, Munch’s bright dot corresponded to the position of Jupiter. Venus was not visible in the sky he painted, and in the 19th century any bright planet after sunset might be called an “evening star.” This narrowed the earliest possible date to July 9, 1893; Munch’s travel records put September 24 as the latest. Weather records further narrowed the date to one of two evenings: August 16 or 23, both of which fit records Pope found for Abendstern .

Impressed, Olson invited Pope to join him; his wife, Marilynn; and others on a research trip to Norway to conduct further investigations into the painting, along with The Storm and other Munch works. She eventually joined ten of Olson’s expeditions, becoming a co-author of six published research papers and appearing in all four of his books . “I created this whole astronomy nerd family,” Pope says of the colleagues she’s met while traveling. “[It’s been] two decades of friendship and research.”

One member of that family is Roger W. Sinnott, a senior editor at Sky & Telescope magazine, where Olson has published many of his results. In 2014, Olson collected some of these articles in Celestial Sleuth: Using Astronomy to Solve Mysteries in Art, History and Literature . More books followed. Celestial Sleuthing: More Mysteries in Art, History and Literature , fourth in the series (which includes a discussion of Friedrich’s The Evening Star ), was published in January 2026.

When approaching a new case, Olson asks four questions about each work examined: Where was the artist located? (Using such tools as computer regressions of lunar, solar and planetary movements combined with angles taken from geologic formations and surviving structures or trees, his group can sometimes determine the artist’s spot within a few feet.) When was the artist there? (Through combined astronomical and historical records, Olson seeks the year, month, day and time, down to the minute if possible.) Which way was the artist looking? (Toward the sky to the north, south, east or west, or toward some direction in between?) What appears in the sky? (For some projects, especially those involving the moon, the object is obvious and may appear in the work’s title, but for others, celestial objects such as comets, meteors or planets are more mysterious.) Searching out evidence such as an artist’s letters and written recollections, other works created in the same vicinity, and period maps, Olson methodically eliminates locations and dates suggested by previous scholars, in the manner of a sharp district attorney destroying a criminal’s alibi.

Of Friedrich’s The Evening Star , he knew that past catalogs had guessed the painting was likely created between 1820 and 1835. Some sources suggested the hill was an invention of the artist, who used it to create an idealized view of Dresden. Olson had read virtually every book on Friedrich, and the uncertainties around this painting, he felt sure, would clear up once he and his team gathered the necessary hard facts.

When Pope wrote to me about the Friedrich painting, she explained that besides helping with astronomical research on the date and location of creation, my photos might corroborate a discovery Olson had made during his investigation of J.M.W. Turner’s Moonlight, a Study at Millbank : Small dots in photographs of paintings were routinely assumed to be dust or image defects and promptly “cleaned up” by photographers—but some of them were probably stars or planets. Perhaps a few unretouched cellphone shots, taken as close as I could get to the actual painting, would clear everything up.

Pope did not have to ask twice. I knew I had to find that dot.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

The current iteration of the Field Naturalists’ Club of Ballarat (FNCB, or the Club) was established in 1952 and continues to thrive, with a healthy and active membership. Since it began, all being well, members have gathered for a monthly Club Meeting and excursion to sites of local natural history interest.

Of the 571 editions of The Ballarat Naturalist available online in the BHL at the time of writing, the December 2025 edition was selected for featuring in this “BHL at 20” Series.

Why? It showcases some of the most celebrated events and people in the Club’s history as events unfolded to bring them together.

Front cover of The Ballarat Naturalist , Dec. 2025 edition. Credit: Field Naturalists’ Club of Ballarat. View on BHL

There is no prerequisite of any specialist knowledge to join the FNCB, just a desire to learn more about nature and a willingness to be involved in efforts to ensure its preservation. Nevertheless, since its inception, FNCB has been most fortunate to benefit from the vast local knowledge of many notable amateur naturalists who have made exceptional contributions to the Club over many decades.

The most anticipated event on the FNCB’s annual Calendar of Activities is the Stella Bedggood Memorial Lecture. It was inaugurated in 1979 in honour of its late namesake in the year after her premature death to cancer. Mrs Bedggood was an outstanding amateur naturalist, self-taught botanist, conservation advocate, educator and photographer who held various offices in the Club including, most notably, the role of Secretary for 13 years.

Each year, the Lecture features a prominent speaker presenting a talk on a natural history topic relevant to the Ballarat region, often with a conservation thread as befits Mrs Bedggood’s legacy. In 2025, the Lecture was even more special for Club members than usual as it featured Roger Thomas who had just been announced as the winner of the prestigious Australian Natural History Medallion (ANHM) 2025. You can view a video recording of the event here .

The December 2025 edition of The Ballarat Naturalist features the write-up of Mr Thomas’s fascinating presentation titled: “ Ballarat’s Nature Noted: A retrospective of Nature writing over four decades ”. It showcased Mr Thomas’s 41 years of weekly “Nature Notes” articles in The Courier (Ballarat), which chronicled the turning of the seasons, special and unusual observations, threats to species and environments, the lifecycles of local flora and fauna, and trends in their abundance and distribution – a veritable gold mine of local natural history.

These introductions collated information from various sources, including the archive of “Nature Notes” articles penned by Roger Thomas for The Courier , historic editions of The Ballarat Naturalist , Dr Susan Kruss’s PhD thesis, A Voice for Nature: A History of the Field Naturalists Club of Ballarat (2024), and the Club’s nomination of Roger for the ANHM 2025.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Wildwood , set in a magical world in the unruly forests bordering Portland, Oregon, is the newest film from animation house Laika . Founded in 2005, the studio became acclaimed for its work on films such as Coraline (2009) and Kubo and the Two Strings (2016). Laika champions practical effects and stop-motion animation —a flipbook-like filmmaking style in which objects are moved frame by frame to create the action seen on screen. At 2 hours and 12 minutes, Wildwood is the longest stop-motion animated film ever made.

The story follows the courageous Prue and her classmate Curtis as she embarks on a fantasy adventure in the forests to find her kidnapped baby brother. Costume designer Deborah Cook developed more than 200 pieces for Wildwood .

After her work on Tim Burton’s Corpse Bride , Cook was approached by Laika to work on Coraline . “It was a definite yes,” she says of relocating her life from London to Portland to be part of what would become an Oscar-nominated film . After that production, she stuck with the studio. She was interested in how much Laika’s CEO Travis Knight, who directed Wildwood , was invested in stop-motion. “I really wanted to be part of that,” Cook says.

Wildwood is based on the 2011 middle-grade fantasy novel of the same name, written by Colin Meloy and illustrated by Carson Ellis.

In 2019, Cook got the Wildwood project and then the world shut down because of the Covid-19 pandemic the following year. Stuck in Portland, the city where the film would take place, the costume designer found herself exploring the region with a whole new set of eyes. All the while, Cook notes that she was “approaching this movie with a really fantastical element plus contemporary Portland.”

Ahead of Wildwood ’s October 23 release, Cook spoke with Smithsonian magazine about the knits and peacoats that she created to adorn the movie’s characters.

What were your first reactions to hearing the breadth of storytelling for Wildwood and the genres you’d pass through to tell the story in costumes?

It didn’t actually feel too daunting because I feel like it’s a reality that we live in Portland anyway. We work in an animation studio in the actual setting of Wildwood , so we live in that contemporary life in Portland, being aware of what everyone wears. It’s very much an outdoorsy kind of area. But then it’s also full of people with a real high level of imagination and creativity. So it felt like I was partway there to understanding that world already.

It was around 2020, literally the start of lockdown, and this was a fantastic anchor because it almost fit what was happening. I could go out to the end of my road and walk around the Wildwood Trail in Forest Park. That was our “permitted activity” to get outside. I saw so much more in the local nature of my environment than I’d ever really properly absorbed. That was fantastic, and the forest there is magnificent. It really felt quite Jurassic to me. The fact that over Covid, there weren’t as many park keepers meant it became more and more unkempt. Things were growing at a rapid rate and really uncontrollably—you could see that escalation weekly, which was magical in itself.

Walking around in the forest at that time, I was very aware of things that I was looking for to discover the vibe of our characters: Like, what would Prue and Curtis feel when they were walking around the forest? What would be normal to them? What would take them out of that world? What is the first thing you would see that would spark a sort of strange curiosity that there’s something mysterious happening that’s out of the ordinary?

Prue is wearing an everyday town coat to start with. She’s very buttoned up and tucked in. She has a few airs and graces, and she thinks she’s a little older and wiser than she is. But when it comes down to the nitty-gritty of having to go out there and rescue her brother, she switches to something that everyone was wearing at that time going into the forest. It’s a little more casual but practical; very, very pragmatic. Everyone has their clothes that would serve them well in a walk around the forest where any weather or climate might come their way. With her trusty boots and hair tied up, she became more of her true self. It revealed her soul a little more, revealing who she really was in a less guarded moment.

Wildwood takes place in a magical world around Portland. How did you begin to approach that world?

[Prue and Curtis] are going into this forest, and they’re seeing people they don’t recognize. They can’t read them very well. What’s been brought into that world is medieval armor, different ways of making clothing that people might have relied on even if there’d been a parallel civilization that we don’t know about. Where did that clothing come from? Was it left behind by previous civilizations?

There wasn’t anything that got into the impassable wilderness from our world. So it was very much fostering that thought process and understanding what could be in the impassable wilderness but also identifying what each different civilization might be wearing, like what those communities and citizens were wearing that identified them and made them separate from each other.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

The MBLWHOI Library’s BHL journey began in 2006 through contributing leadership, technical expertise, and hands-on librarian effort to the exciting BHL start-up period. Today and for many years, a quiet but deliberate process has taken place towards introducing grade school through graduate level students and researchers to the Biodiversity Heritage Library. This happens in a single one-hour-long class students attend in the MBLWHOI Library where BHL is presented as an online tool that students can learn to use to extend their research studies of bound paper science books and journals.

These classes use BHL content to show students (the youngest of whom nowadays have minimal experience using paper books) the look and tactile feel of books that are hundreds of years old, while referencing the BHL digital examples showing the interface of print and online in science publishing, such as bound-in-volume foldouts (foldouts are bound book pages sized larger than the size of the pages of a book and folded into the book). A quick foldout example is shown below, in a plate bound before the first page of volume 8, no. 81 (1672), Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London : An attempt of a new kind of telescope invented by Mr. Isaac Newton .

Part of the unique BHL and in-library viewing experience is looking at and being able to download and understand vital details, such as illustrations contained in foldouts. View in BHL .

The Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) was founded in the village of Woods Hole, Massachusetts, in 1888 as America’s first private marine biological laboratory. In 1930, scientists at MBL and the nascent oceanography community collaborated in the founding of another of the key Woods Hole science laboratories, the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI).

In the 1870s, Spencer Fullerton Baird, Secretary of the then recently founded Smithsonian Institution followed through on a charge from US President Ulysses S. Grant to found the US Bureau of Fisheries. Through this process, Baird discovered that the regional waters surrounding the village of Woods Hole are particularly rich in marine biodiversity. This natural phenomenon is influenced by the mixing of warm Gulf Stream currents from the southeast with the cool Labrador currents of the northeast. Secretary Baird also realized that some of the strongest tidal currents on the East Coast of the US are located just off Woods Hole Harbor. See the historical note below from A biological survey of the waters of Woods Hole and vicinity , Sumner, F., Osburn, R., Cole, L. (1911) Bulletin of the Bureau of Fisheries v.31 p.12:

“… Many years ago, Woods Hole was selected by Prof. Baird as the most promising spot upon our coast for the commencement of a scientific study of fisheries problems. From the very outset he gathered about him a staff of naturalists of the type that was dominant in that generation — men eager to seek out every living thing concealed beneath the waves, to describe and figure and name…”

To this day we encourage students to explore the late-summer biodiversity of the waters surrounding Woods Hole by dropping a fishing line to explore the possible diversity of the catch.

On the wall of the office of the MBLWHOI Library is an 1873 poster that was originally hung in the classroom of the Anderson School of Natural History (1873–1875). This poster, with the quote below, was often attributed to Anderson School founder and Harvard professor Louis Agassiz. “Study nature, not books” was a statement reflective of learning through personal experience. The Anderson School of Natural History, which operated on Penikese Island near Woods Hole, was an antecedent of the Marine Biological Laboratory. This school was purposely sited on a postage-stamp-sized island so the students could do their work without summer seaside community distractions. The poster’s statement “Study nature, not books” is appropriate to the MBLWHOI Library and science study in Woods Hole because “learning science by doing science” is how research has traditionally taken place in Woods Hole. We tell the students attending the brief rare books class that we will revisit this quote later in the short class.

1873 poster, “Study nature not books”, from the MBLWHOI Library. Photo courtesy of the author.

In the MBLWHOI Library rare books collection, in Volume 1, number 8 (1666) of Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London , is an article titled: Directions for sea-men bound for far Voyages . Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London is considered the oldest continuously published scientific journal in the Western world. Its founding in the mid-1660s reflects efforts by scientists and science-interested people in Western Europe and the British Isles to create and document knowledge, compiling references to science experiments and meeting in person or through detailed correspondence to discuss often differing viewpoints on scientific matters. The journal articles which made up Philosophical Transactions were often letters received by the Royal Society, and the proceedings of meetings that took place at the Royal Society in London. Highlighted below are the first few lines of the article, Directions for Sea-men bound for far Voyages :

“It being the design of the Royal Society, for the better attaining the end of their institution, to study Nature rather than Books , and from the observations, made of the phenomena and effects she presents, to compose such a history of Her, as may hereafter serve to build a solid and useful philosophy upon…to think upon and set down Directions for sea-men going into the East- & West-Indies, the better to capacitate them for making such observations abroad, as may be pertinent and suitable for their purpose…”

Directions for Sea-men bound for far Voyages , from Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London , vol. 1, no. 8, p. 140 (1666). View in BHL .

Students can read on to see that article details are attributed to “Master Rooke”, Lawrence Rooke, a 17th-century English mathematician and astronomer from Gresham College in London. The article goes on to instruct “sea-men bound for far voyages” on what they should be doing to study nature hands-on, meaning: keeping a diary that would include using the instruments of the day to detail the data associated with their voyage: the compass, dipping needles, (another magnetic-field measuring device), visually taking note of the ebbing and flowing of the tides while noting ordinary and extraordinary events, mapmaking, depth measuring, to record and describe weather and astronomical observations, as well as filling and weighing bottles of seawater from different ocean depths.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
Since long before the United States was formed, the continent has been the home of Native American people, including the Lakota, Navajo, Sioux, Cherokee, Apache, Dakota and others. The names of those tribes still designate our waterways (the Potomac River, Lake Erie), national parks (Shenandoah and Denali) and even some states (Michigan and Ohio). Native American communities have, of course, contributed more than geographical names and remain a vital part of the fabric of American life. About 7.4 million self-identified Native Americans live in the United States today, and many continue the rich and meaningful traditions of their heritage.

Jeff Campagna is a photo editor at Smithsonian magazine. You can follow him on Instagram at @jeffcampagna .

Tracy Scott Forson is a senior editor at Smithsonian magazine.

items.title: Collections as data: Transcribing the ornithological observations of Walter Faxon
items.author: Joe deVeer
items.summary: Walter Faxon’s ornithological field journals contain thousands of bird observations spanning more than three decades. Now digitized and transcribed using AI-assisted tools, these handwritten records are unlocking historical biodiversity data that could help us better understand environmental change over time.

items.cleanReaderHtml:
This post is part of BHL at 20: Treasures from the Biodiversity Heritage Library , a series contributed by members of the BHL community, highlighting remarkable works from across the collection in celebration of its 20th anniversary.

With the world facing the dual crisis of climate change and biodiversity loss, the emergence of the Biodiversity Heritage Library (BHL) 20 years ago was timely. Over that 20-year span, BHL has grown to become “the world’s largest open access digital library for biodiversity literature and archives” 1 with a corpus of over 64 million pages. This vast corpus is also a repository of historical biodiversity data waiting to be extracted and used to inform a better understanding of anthropogenic effects on climate, the environment, and life on Earth.

Portraits of Walter Faxon taken at graduation from Harvard (1871) and later in life (1896). Harvard College; Heliotype Printing Co.

One “dataset” recently added to BHL is the Ernst Mayr Library ’s (EML) collection of Walter Faxon’s ornithological field journals , field notebooks and bird lists . Faxon (February 4, 1848 – August 10, 1920) was a native of Massachusetts. He was an Assistant Professor of Zoology at Harvard University from 1872 to 1886. Faxon specialized in the study of crustaceans and was Curator of the Invertebrate Department at Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology (MCZ) for 46 years (1874–1920). He focused his work primarily on the Museum’s collections of Crustacea and Mollusca.

Pencil sketch of Pagurus sp. (hermit crab) first zoeal stage. Drawn by Walter Faxon on 3 August 1881. From the Ernst Mayr Library and Archives of the Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University.

Ornithology was an avocation for Faxon, but he pursued it with the same level of professionalism with which he approached his curatorial work. He was a Fellow of the American Ornithologists’ Union from 1901–1904. “His long experience in the field [nearly 60 years] and his alertness of eye, ear and mind, as well as his scrupulous care to avoid error, combined to make him one of the best equipped and accurate of field ornithologists – the identification of a bird by him was never questioned.” 2 This inspires confidence in the authenticity of the historical data Faxon left for us, now accessible via the BHL.

The Faxon collection in the Ernst Mayr Library is relatively small, consisting of just over 2,200 pages of manuscript field journals, bird lists, field notebooks, correspondence, eight pencil drawings of Arthropoda and Crustacea, and some additional miscellaneous items. The EML also holds a large collection of William Brewster’s papers that include 145 letters to and from Faxon. Though not voluminous, Faxon’s field journals, bird lists and field notebooks (totaling 1,640 pages) record thousands of bird observations with species name, date, locality, number of individuals seen, and often additional information such as sex, life stage, and vocalization. These species occurrence data, compiled over 33 years (1886–1919), is arguably the greatest asset of Faxon’s collection. Aggregated with similar data from other sources around the world, the resulting dataset will help provide a clear picture of biodiversity change over time, informing efforts to mitigate accelerating species decline.

BHL is well positioned to facilitate development of an aggregated global dataset. By providing the infrastructure and tools to host transcript files for manuscript materials, making the text searchable and scientific names discoverable, BHL promotes extraction of species occurrence data.

With the goal of including Faxon’s data with BHL exports to the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), the EML has digitized and transcribed his ornithological observations. In 2025, the collection was digitized with the support of the Harvard Library Collections Digitization Program under the theme of Climate Change. In 2026, the EML was chosen to host a Pforzheimer Fellow to investigate the use of AI-powered tools to transcribe Faxon’s field journals, notebooks, and species lists.

Our Fellow, Mohit Mandal , a Harvard PhD candidate in Anthropology, worked on this project from June 1 to August 31, 2026. He began by evaluating ChatGPT and Google Gemini to determine which model would be best suited for the Faxon materials. Mohit found Gemini to have the edge in accuracy, but more constrained by file upload limits and not as user-friendly, as it works only with Google Workspace tools (e.g., no support for Microsoft Word). He found ChatGPT to be more flexible with follow-up prompting and had success retaining consistency by training the model according to his specifications. Based on this assessment he chose ChatGPT for the project. The initial transcripts were then verified using a different AI tool, Claude, to draw upon the two models’ complementary capabilities and improve overall accuracy.

The screenshots below display page images alongside transcript text in the BHL book viewer. Overall, the results are impressive with pages reviewed thus far revealing relatively few errors. The goal of transcribing nearly 2,000 manuscript pages was achieved. The Pforzheimer Fellowship ended just one week before this writing, so we have not yet had time to calculate an accuracy metric. Some of the difficulties encountered are typical for transcription of handwritten material: notes written in pencil with smudges; marginal text written at an angle (poorly transcribed and, in some instances, not recognized by AI), etc.

One of the greatest challenges was training ChatGPT to capture tiny interlinear numbers and symbols that Faxon would place above the main lines of text (i.e., between lines). This interlinear text would record such things as the number of individual birds of a species seen on a given date, whether the birds were singing, and if they were in a flock. Mohit posits that the difficulty capturing this text may be a consequence of line-spacing constraints with word processors such as Microsoft Word and Google Docs. Ultimately, he was able to preserve the interlinear notations by formatting them as superscript text (Figures 3 and 4).

Left: Extract from Faxon’s April 1890 bird list highlighting his use of interlinear characters. Transcribed with ChatGPT-5.5 Thinking. From the Ernst Mayr Library and Archives of the Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University. Right: Transcript of the extract with interlinear characters. ChatGPT would often miss these characters, especially on pages with difficult handwriting or on dates appended with more than one character. AI transcription of such characters requires further refinement.

Page 1 of Faxon’s Field Journal, v.1 (1889–91) , with transcript in BHL book viewer. Transcribed with ChatGPT-5.5 Pro. From the Ernst Mayr Library and Archives of the Museum of Comparative Zoology, Harvard University.
